On the Orders of the Day:

Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb) if it is correct that last summer he held a quiet inquiry into the operations of an organization, or alleged organization, engaged at American ports in the business of adulterating Canadian grain for export. If so, what were the results of the inquiry, and when may we expect a report thereon to be tabled?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext: I never heard of such an organization until to-day.
No inquiries, then were held last summer by the minister or by his department as to such adulteration?
I am not sure what my hon. friend refers to. If he would be more specific I might be able to give him the information he desires.
Perhaps I can put my question directly. Were any inquiries made by the minister or his department last summer into the adulteration of Canadian grain at American ports?

Mr. Speaker, last year we had a complaint from the London Com Exchange that Canadian grain reaching London was not up to standard. I met the members in their exchange hall, London, and the chairman made it clear that they had no complaints against Canadian grain reaching England from Canadian ports; their complaints were against Canadian grain reaching England through certain United States ports. We instructed the Board of Grain Commissioners -one of the inspectors went along with them -to make an actual survey of the conditions there affecting the receiving and the loading of grain going out to those ports. The chairman of the board and the chief grain inspector have gone over with the idea that they will reach there about the time the first ships arrive from Canada and from the United States. They will make inquiries and observations with a view to giving the government information regarding the condition of the grain that reaches the other side.

Mr. GARDINER.: I understood the minister to say that they had asked the Board of Grain Commissioners to make inquiry in United States ports. What we desire to know is what was the result of that inquiry.

Well, offhand, the information that was brought back to us confirmed our own view, namely, that we have no control in the United States over grain, once it is cleared from Buffalo. It is true -the grain goes through the United States in bond, but that is for the protection of the people of the United States themselves, So it comes down to this-if grain is shipped to Liverpool direct from Canada and then from Liverpool to France and the complaint comes to us from France that it is not up to standard, we have no control over it because it had reached the Liverpool .port-beyond our country.

Amount not exceeding $73,000,000 to meet expenditures made or indebtedness incurred (where amounts available from net operating earnings may be insufficient) by or on behalf of the Canadian National Railway Company, hereinafter called "the company", or any company specified in the First Schedule to the act incorporating the Canadian National Railway Company, being chapter 13 of the Statutes of Canada, 1919, or by the company in respect of any railways, properties or works entrusted to the company from time to time under the provisions of section 11 of the

said chapter 13 of the Statutes of Canada, 1919, or bv or on behalf of any company specified or referred to in chapter 13 of the Statutes of Canada, 1920; or any one or more of them, on any of the following accounts :-
(a)	Operating deficits whenever incurred or ascertained.
(b)	Acquisition of property, materials and supplies.
(c)	Interest and sinking funds on notes, securities or obligations.
(d)	Principal and interest of maturing or matured loans secured or unsecured.
(e)	Construction and betterments.
(f)	Co-ordination or consolidation of railway lines and facilities.
(g)	Guarantees of securities.
The amount herein authorized may be applied from time to time, in the discretion of the Governor in Council:-
(a)	To meet expenditures made or indebtedness incurred by the Company in respect of railways, properties and works entrusted to the company as aforesaid.
(b)	By way of loans in cash, or by way of guarantee, or partly one way and partly the other, subject, however, as follows:-
If by way of loans, the amount or amounts advanced shall be repayable on demand, with interest at the rate fixed by the Governor in Council, from time to time, payable half-yearly, secured if and when directed by the Governor in Council by mortgage or mortgages upon such properties in such form and containing such terms and conditions, not inconsistent herewith, as the Governor in Council may approve.
If by way of guarantee, any such guarantee may be of the principal and interest of the notes and obligations or securities of one or more of the said companies specified by the Governor in Council, and may be signed by the Minister of Finance, on behalf of His Majesty, in such form and on such terms and conditions as the Governor in Council may determine to be appropriate and applicable thereto, $73,000,000.

In connection with the matter under discussion last night, the purchase of the two-million-dollar hotel in Paris, I would like to ask the minister whether or not the board of directors of the Canadian National Railway Company have approved of the purchase as made.	[DOT]
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals): Some two months ago the question of getting proper quarters in Paris, I am informed, was discussed at a meeting of the board, and approved. I do not think this special transaction has yet been brought before the board for approval.

Will the minister give the
committee an idea of the service to be rendered to the Canadian National, or to the Canadian nation for that matter, by this purchase?

The only answer I can
give* to my hon. friend is that the Canadian National has had no headquarters in Paris and it is the judgment of the Canadian National Company that such headquarters are greatly needed for the good of the Canadian National system.

Supply-Railways-C.N.R.

Has the Canadian National
similar headquarters in the other European headquarters-Rome, Berlin, Stockholm? If not, why purchase one in Paris and not in the others?

The Canadian Pacific
Railway have headquarters in Paris. I do not know about the others. Paris is considered a very central point of European trade. It is, in a way, the hub of the wheel.

There is this great difference between the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National: the Canadian Pacific has steamship lines across the ocean and I understand also has railroad systems on the Continent. I could understand that they would require headquarters of this character. But I cannot see how the Canadian National would require them.

I have never heard of
the Canadian Pacific having railway lines on the Continent. They have their own steamship lines; and the Canadian National has connection with the Cunard and White Star lines.

Then, do I understand
that this purchase in Paris is merely "Keeping up with the Joneses," so to speak? Is that. the service that is expected by it?

How is this figure of
$73,000,000 made up? I understand that about $58,000,000 is required to cover the deficit. Is this for the deficit on last year's operating?

I regret I was unable to
hear the last part of my hon. friend's remark, but I understand that he is asking how the $73,000,000 is made up. I will give the totals: For the Canadian Government Railways, $5,772,941; Canadian Northern, $36,906,826.64; Grand Trunk, $20,000,000; Grand Trunk Pacific, $10,320,232.36; operating deficit, estimate for next year-which we think is very liberal, but provision must be made-$10,000,000; interest and other sundry charges, $22,821,260.34; refunding and sinking funds, $8,184,699.33; capital betterment and equipment, $31,994,-040.33;-making a total of $73,000,000.

Have the department taken into consideration the matter of adjusting the capitalization of these railways? The Canadian Government railways, of course, have no capitalization, but the others have. Has the idea of writing off or readjusting the value to bring it down to the actual value been considered at all?

That suggestion has been made in several quarters. I think the former
leader of the Progressive party urged it very strongly. It would not in any way reduce the liability of the country. If you owe so much money you would still owe it whether you write down the capitalization or not. But it is a matter for investigation. This has to be borne in mind, however,-as my hon. friend has pointed out, there is quite a proportion of the Canadian National system now known as the Government Railways, the capitalization of which is not considered in the indebtedness of the railway, so if the Canadian National system outside of the Government Railways is over-capitalized as some contend, you have to offset that in making your calculations. The amount of capital invested in the Government Railways is about $440,000,000, if I remember correctly.

I have compiled some figures that are rather illuminating. The Canadian National-and when I say the Canadian National in this case I am including the Grand Trunk but excluding the Canadian Government railways-had net earnings last year of $193,171,000, and against that interest or fixed charges of $62,454,000; while the Canadian Pacific, with earnings nearly as high, $186,665,000, has fixed charges of only $13,348,000. Taking our roads separately I find that the Canadian Northern for 1922 had gross earnings of only $1.85 for every dollar of fixed charges; the Grand Trunk Pacific had $2.17 earnings for every dollar of fixed charges; the Canadian Government railways had $1.79 of earnings for every dollar of capitalization; and the Grand Trunk had $6.95 of earnings for every dollar of fixed charges. And the Canadian Pacific had a revenue of $13.98 for every dollar of fixed charges. I might say in connection with the Canadian Government Railways that I arrived at the fixed charges by computing 51 per cent interest on the investment of $414,000,000. I should like to quote at this point from an editorial in the Manitoba Free Press regarding the capitalization of the railways. It says:
The time has now come to consider seriously the proposition which has been frequently advanced during the past two or three years, to cut down the capitalization of the system to a point where it will represent the actual value of the road. . . It will not be denied that the capitalization of the Canadian National railway is far in excess of the physical value of the road. In this huge mountain of debt are embedded all the railway blunders of Canada sinoe the first railway was built.
Further on it makes this reference to the effect on the operations of the road:
Supply-Railways-C Jf.R.

Of the operators of the Canadian National railway miracles should not be demanded. They cannot be expected to make surpluses sufficient to pay interest charges upon the present combined capitalization of the system. Faced with the certainty that every year there will be a huge deficit the directors of the system will inevitably get into the frame of mind which finds expression in the phrase: "What's the use?'' If there's bound to be a deficit anyway, why worry whether it is ten or twenty million dollars.
But, given a just valuation of the road, the directors can be told that they must meet the fixed charges or make way for others who can. They will have a target to aim at and they will be expected to hit it. This will be much more exhilarating and inspiring than shooting arrows into a box.
We have plenty of precedent for such action. The whole capitalization of the Canadian Government railways-that is, what are called in the statement the Canadian Government railways, the Intercolonial, the Transcontinental and the Prince Edward Island railway-'has been wiped off and charged up to the public debt. I notice also that an item of $2,394,000 spent on the Canadian Pacific between Ottawa and Quebec was transferred to the public debt in 1898. I think the minister would do well to give this matter serious consideration.

It is a large question, of course. I imagine that the government, if it thought wise, could perhaps deal with the securities held by itself, although that would not relieve the financial obligation of the country at all, but the securities in the hands of the public would have to remain and the liability be held sacred.

After listening to the minister last night and to the discussion which then took place I have been trying to ascertain the situation in connection with this Paris transaction. I presume the minister will not deny that there must be somewhere in the statutes authority conferred upon the president or the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways to enter into a transaction of this character? I should like him, in the first place, to refer me to the section in the act which confers authority upon the president of the railway or upon the board of directors; secondly, I would like to know exactly what the position is in regard to that $2,000,000 transaction. Is it out of the control now of the National Railways and out of the control of Sir Henry Thornton? Has the money been paid over? What is the situation?

I explained that fully last night, but I will explain it again. The building was required, so the president of the board cons:dered. In his judgment the transaction would have to take place very quickly or the opportunity would be lost. The Canadian

National Railways financed this gentleman in Paris to get possession of the building. The money was deposited in the Bank of Toronto, just as money in like cases has been deposited by other governments for other purposes; and that deposit in the Bank of Toronto allowed the man in Paris to finance the building. In other words, the Canadian National for the time being financed the transaction in order to get control of this building. And they took a mortgage, I am told, in the London office, to protect themselves.
A mortgage from whom?
I have mentioned that three or four times already. I do not think my hon. friend can pronounce the name when I say it-Aronovici.

I confess that I find difficulty in understanding the situation. Why take a mortgage? Why should not the title have been taken in the name of the Canadian National Railways? Why take a mortgage in favour of the Canadian National Railways?

I see what my hon. friend is at now. As I understand it, the board did not intend to retain possession of this building. However, I see what my hon. friend is after. He will pardon me, I hope, if I cannot grasp these legal niceties as quickly as legal gentlemen can. But if that had been done I know he would probably have risen immediately and said there had been a violation of the act of 1919 in that the Canadan National is not empowered .to build or extend lines or to make any extended capital expenditure without an order in council. The property was not bought in the name of the Canadian National Railways, but in the name of this gentleman whose name I have tried to pronounce, who was financed, temporarily only, by the Governor in Council.
Then I take it, from what the minister says, that the title to the property does stand in the name of Aronovici, and the mortgage is with the Canadian National Railways?
That is as I understand it.
For the full amount of the sum advanced?
Yes.

I would like to ask the minister if he can point to the section of the act which authorizes a transaction of this character?

Supply-Railways-C.N.R.
The act is negative and positive in different places.
Oh, no.

That is absolutely right. My hon. friends know that the act gives .certain powers and declines to give other powers. Will my hon. friend tell me of any section in the act which enjoins the president from doing anything of this kind?
Oh, oh.

I had not the advantage of being here last night, but I have read Hansard since and I must commence by saying that there was revealed last night the most extraordinary transaction, I think, ever disclosed in this parliament. I have difficulty in finding words to describe the conduct of the board. In so far as the minister is concerned his responsibility apparently arose after the transaction was complete, and his error [DOT]consists in condoning the transaction and expressing approval of it in this House. A knowledge of-I had almost said of law-but a knowledge of the plain, simple facts connected with, or rather which constituted, the basis adopted by this parliament for the control of our National railways is necessary to comprehend the seriousness of what has been done. When this countiy found itself compelled to take over large railways-railways which could not stand up unless they were taken over-we had to find some way, some system, whereby we could at once get [DOT]operation on business lines unaffected and uninterfered with by political considerations, and at the same time keep in the hands of the representatives of the people that fundamental control of general policy and of expenditure that necessarily the people of Canada would insist on where their own money is involved. Now the method adopted was this-and it is the very kernel, it is the very essence of the whole National Railway Act -that is so far as operation, ordinary operation, is concerned the board of directors elected by the Governor in Council should be in exactly the same position as any other board of directors elected by their shareholders, but there the control of the board of directors ended. In so far as policy and in so far as capital investment were concerned the board of directors could recommend and could do no more. The line was drawn between capital investment and operation. It is not a legal nieety; no one can escape the issue by merely hiding behind a lack of "knowledge of law; it is as plain and naked a principle as anybody has ever seen. Let
me repeat. As read in part by the member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) last night the National Railway Act provides that neither the board of directors nor the manager has any power to expend or pledge the money of this country for capital investment, save with the antecedent authorization of the Governor in Council. And the Governor in Council had its powers only when the money for the express purpose had been voted by this House.
What has happened? The manager of the Canadian National Railways desired to buy with the money of our railways, which means the money of this country, an hotel in Paris -to be converted I presume into some immense structure there-in order that Canada may get "on the main street" of Paris, to use the graphic language of the Minister of Railways. I do not know at what stage the device was adopted, but I have a suspicion that the circuitous plan finally used was not the original intent of Sir Henry Thornton and the management. I fancy it was when the fundamental legal position came before their eyes in its fuH strength that this device was adopted; to call it a subterfuge is to honour it. They buy the property in the name of one Aronovici who is their own servant in Paris. The minister says they could not buy it as a capital expenditure and take the title to the company; to do so is against the law. The right to do so has been denied by this parliament. But the minister thinks it is all right for them to buy it with the company's money in the name of Aronovici, and the minister passes his blessing on the conduct of Sir Henry Thornton adopting a subterfuge of that sort. I do not admit for a moment they had a right to buy this property in the name of Aronovici or of anyone else, and I question very much if they had the legal opinion of any lawyer of repute that such a thing could without a previous vote of parliament be done. But with or without a lawyer's opinion the people of this country will not stand for subterfuge of that sort to get round the provisions of an act of parliament. The parties go to the Bank of Toronto, they take the money of the people of this country and lodge it in the bank; and then the bank sends that money over to Aronovici to buy an hotel in Paris. What have they for it? They have not anything save the Paris hotel. They buy the property and then they set to work to get some syndicate to take it over-I mean the board, I mean Sir Henry Thornton-and so far as we are informed we do not know up to this hour in parliament whether there

Supply-Railways-C.N.R.

is any syndicate bound to take it over or not. If there is we do not know who compose the syndicate.
Now, what is the position? We have $2,000,000 of capital expenditure invested in a Paris hotel, not only against the intent but against the plainest wording of an act of parliament, an act as plain as this or any other parliament ever enacted-money taken from the purposes to which it was applied by a statute of parliament, misappropriated from these purposes and invested in a Paris hotel: Or; without the knowledge of the government we have money loaned on the credit of a syndicate we do not know, money of the Canadian people loaned to a syndicate whose names we are denied. Which is the better of the two horns of the dilemma? This thing is a scandal, this is an outrage, and when this became known to the minister Sir Henry Thornton should have been called to book at once. When the minister comes to this House and says that the thing is all right because the property is bought in the name of Aronovici instead of in the name of the Canadian National Railways I do not think he does justice to himself. I venture to say, because I have a profound respect for the Minister of 'Railways, that when Sir Henry Thornton first disclosed to him what he had done his language to that gentleman was not like what it has been in this House. But he had not the courage to do to Sir Henry Thornton what he should have done, and to reprimand his conduct now before this House. What right, I want to know, has he to put his hand into the treasury of Canada and apply $2,000,000 to get the National Railways "on the main street" of Paris? No one can argue for a moment that it is in accordance with the intent of that act. It is diametrically opposed to the law, and everybody knows it, to invest capital money without the consent of the government and without previous appropriation by this House. But first, had we not better get on the main street of Canada before we get on the main street of Paris? Where are we to-day? We have the property. We have it in our own name in this shape: Mr. Aronovici has the title and has mortgaged the property to us. As everybody knows, this course is merely a substitute for having it in the name of the Canadian National Railways. We hold the property to-day, a property that is a capital investment in Paris; and all we have is a hope, annexed to which there is not a line, so far as this House has been informed, that some time some people over in New York will take it off our hands. Who the people in New York are we do not know, and I think the

minister said last night he did not know himself. That is the position Canada is in. And the minister thinks it is all right.
Is Sir Henry Thornton to have power to repeat this performance? If he has power to go into the treasury to the extent of $2,000,000, he has power to go into the treasury to the extent of $20,000,000. He can pledge this country in Paris, Berlin, South America, or anywhere he pleases, for the whole of the moneys at the disposal of the Canadian National Railways in capital account, as long as he does it by the circuitous sinuosity he adopted in this case, and the minister will think it is all right. The minister should have denounced it and he should have dealt with Sir Henry Thornton on the spot. No board of directors, no matter who they are, has power to do any such thing, nor should be given such power, nor should be condoned for doing it. The country has not very much confidence in the board of directors, if they have any. The proportion of them who should have been appointed is small. The country has welcomed and has given a fair opportunity to Sir Henry Thornton. But the confidence of the country in Sir Henry Thornton will not last much longer after they know of this transaction; and furthermore the country's confidence in the minister will be seriously shattered when it finds he condoned a transaction of this kind on the floor of this House.

I do not know that I can add anything to what I have said. I think I said last night that if I had been doing it, probably I would not have done it that way. However, the question turns largely on the legality of the transaction, and I gave as an authority the adviser of the president, Mr. Ruel. We all have a high opinion of him. And his reply to me, when asked if this was a legal transaction, was that it certainly was. As to the advisability of it, I said before that I would not have done it that way. But I am convinced that the necessity of getting headquarters in Paris is very essential, in order that we may get our share of the traffic. My right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) says we are not on the main street in Canada. Well, there was quite a criticism because we insisted on staying on the main street in Toronto. But the way to get on the main street in Canada is not altogether through our own people or their products. One way is to get more people, and the other way is to get the traffic of other lines as much as possible. My own view is, disregarding for the moment the discussion of how this property was obtained, that it is absolutely essential that, in the

Supply-Railways-C .N.R.
centres where traffic is to be obtained, the Canadian National must have a prominent place. It must have a place in the centre of the business district where the people will recognize not only Canada but the Canadian National Railways. I can refer my hon. friend to a case, not on all fours with this, because the government did it. I refer to the letting of the contract of the new Halifax harbour works, which to my mind was all wrong-but that is only a matter of opinion. If the right hon. gentleman will look up the facts in that case he will find that there was no appropriation by parliament and no money. The government borrowed and placed in the bank $300,000, and sent agents to buy up certain properties, to establish the value. Well, it was the government that was doing it. They had no order in council authorizing it to be done, so I am informed. It was done, as to the details, just as this transaction was done. However, that is not important. That is the way they raised the money. I want to point out something my right hon. friend has said himself. I want parliament to thoroughly understand that I do not approve, or would not approve, of any transaction about which there was the least shade of dishonesty or departure from rectitude, I would not care with whom I might have to disagree. But in this case there is no evidence of such a thing. There was the desire on the part of the Canadian National to obtain a certain property which other people were endeavouring to obtain. Perhaps my right hon. friend knows who they are. Sir Henry Thornton might have been impetuous in his anxiety to get this property on which he had his eye for something else. But outside of that, there is nothing in the transaction at all to point, to anything in the least wrong. The Canadian National Railways Act of 1919 gave the Canadian National board pretty wide powers. My right hon. friend rightly says that the Board of Directors of the Canadian National, including its president, was given the same, powers as are given to the directorate and president of a private company.
Over operation.
He did not say that.
Yes, that is what I said distinctly.

Well, I will leave it,that way, but I think it goes further. I am going to put him on the same plane. It was argued last night-and I think rightly so-that the president of a private company ought to have the approval of the shareholders for a trans-
233i
action of this kind. That was argued by two or three of my hon. friends on the other side of the House. The practice is, as everybody knows, that the president of a large private corporation or some person acting for and with him, exercises very extensive powers, and while he proceeds in a case of this kind, to purchase property, he would purchase it first, and ask for the approval afterwards, because if he did not do that, the price would be greatly enhanced when he came to purchase the building in the name of a big company, and I imagine the same thing would happen in this case. I admit frankly to my mind capital expenditure, if this were held to be a purchase by the Canadian National, could not be made except by the consent of the shareholders, the shareholders being the Governor in Council in this case. The practice-and I suppose Sir Henry Thornton followed the practice that he followed when he was with the great English company-is for the executive in such cases as this to make their arrangements first, depending on the approval of the shareholders. But I want to quote my right hon. friend, the leader of the Opposition, with reference to a position he took a few days ago, not on this question, but on the powers of the board. I know my hon. friend will say that that applied to operation only. That may technically be correct.
Absolutely.
I would rather say "technically."
Read section 11.

I am going to read thespeech of my right hon. friend-it overrides^ section 11, maybe-to point out to the members of this committee that I would take it from his words uttered there and, I think, correctly that even in this transaction Sir Henry Thornton was not going very far afield from the principle laid down,-with the fact that the minister was not in a position to give details, being advised by the president that this would not be in the interest of the Canadian National at the present time. I think this was confirmed by my right hon. friend's words uttered the other day, although he will still insist that they meant only matters of operation.
What date was that?

Hansard, May 4. I think I was engaged in the discussion myself and my right hon. friend as well. In reply to something that I had remarked, my right hon. friend said.
Supply-Railways-C.N.R.

Nothing could be a greater contrast than the position of the minister to that of his friends when they were on this side of the House. I wish to take exactly the same position that I took then: I do not believe in details of management being revealable every day or discussable in the House of Commons, and never did. At the same time I realize, as I realized when in power, that there are some matters in connection with which the details might be brought before the House at the proper time-when that might be done without interfering with the actual day to day management, and when all the doings of the company could be scrutinized by hon. members.
The question arises:	Was this a part of
the management of the Canadian National system open for discussion? I submit, taking the broad meaning of my right hon. friend's words, it would come within that category.

Is the hon. member
seriously intimating that this is ordinary everyday, day to day management of a railway?
My right hon. friend went further.

That is what my hon.
friend read.
I am going to read more.
It will be just as good.

If everything is done legally, nothing out of the ordinary, everything within the four corners of the act, then I think anything that would enhance the value of the line as regards earning power might be considered as part of the management of the railway. My right hon. friend continued:
While management is on and while they are hiring this man and firing that man-
I think he is using my words there.
-buying coal here and refusing to buy it there, we admitted and argued strenuously that it was impossible to have these things subjected to daily scrutiny, but we always said that the time came when the House had a right to inquire into everything in management, and we asked that committee to ascertain when that time came and how these matters could be brought before the House.
That has reference to the argument under the late government for a committee to which these things might be referred. The committee would have to be very small if all the information would not get out. I have great faith in human nature, but I never knew a committee of any proportions that did not have on it someone who had a friend to tell the information to quietly, and one might almost as well have the information on the records of this House. My right hon. friend said further:	[DOT]
But we went this far ourselves: That this was the place where railway expenditures should be made
IMr. Graham.]
known, but made known at a time when they would not harass the management of the system. Consequently the committee was appointed.
I read these things just to point out to my right hon. friend that less than a week ago he took the ground that as regards details- he did not say details, but as regards the management of a railway, and information concerning it, there was a time to give out the information, and that was when this would not embarrass the management of the road. I do not think I can add anything further to what I have said. My right hon. friend asked me a question, and I think I can go this far with him. I shall be perfectly frank with him. If Sir Henry Thornton or the board could exercise this authority in large degree whenever he saw fit to do so, I think, without saying any more, I should be accurate in the remark that it is not likely to be exercised again.

I feel a measure of satisfaction in that there is a note of repentance evident now in the speech of the minister. I must congratulate him on the selection he made of an extract from my own speech made on the 4th May.
I beg pardon; I thought it was the 4th June.

The 4th May. It would be just the same as if it were the 4th May, 1919; he would not find an iota of difference. I could not, if I had it to do again, express my meaning a particle more clearly and in a way more applicable to this case
4 p.m. than I expressed it in the extract read by the minister. Certainly! In matters of management! under section 11, the term "management" is defined in the clearest possible way and the board has authority as regards matters affected by section II, matters of day to day management and operation. I used the term specifically- why, I even went further in what the minister quoted-I described what day to day management implied; I gave instances: the buying of coal, hiring of men, firing of men. All those things I did not think should come before parliament-things of that character as they were going on. But I added later on there would come time even for that.
How does that kind of thing affect a transaction of this sort? They are as remote from it .as the stars are from this earth; they have nothing in common with it. Section 23 provides that the directors shall have nothing to do in the way of final authority save by direction of the Governor in Council and after a vote of this House with new invest-

ment or const,ruction and manifestly one such thing, is to buy a hotel in Paris. You could not imagine a more outstanding instance. What I find fault with the minister for is that he approved in this House what was done and gave carte blanche to Sir Henry Thornton. No general manager is entitled to confidence who would be guilty of an action of this sort. I do not say yet that he is guilty of wrongful intent.	The route he pursued showed that he was not acting in accordance with the law. Think of Sir Henry Thornton taking upon himself the duty of manager of this system and not knowing the simple truth that as regards capital investment he had to come to the Governor in Council for authority and that the money for the purpose must previously have been voted by parliament. Nothing will convince any hon. member who is sincere that Sir Henry Thornton does not know as well as any living man that he has to have that prior authority, and that the Governor in Council has to have the prior vote of Parliament. But he goes to work and he takes the money of the Canadian National railway, which money was put there by the Minister of Finance for purposes voted by this parliament last session, and he sends $2,000,000 of it through the agent of the Bank of Toronto to Paris to buy a hotel. This is what he has done, and this is what he is accountable for to this country. We are going to have to pay for this transaction. The prospect of escape looks very dark to me; but escape or no escape, the thing is wrong and should have been denounced by the government.
But how are we going to escape? By taking enough space in this building and paying enough rental to make it worth while for an unknown syndicate in New York to take it off our hands. We have an option. We have financed-the word is hardly appropriate- we have bought it and we hope to sell it. We hope to get rid of it to some people, we do not know to whom, but we have got to pay the $2,000,000. The money is already gone. Still we are told we have an option from this unknown syndicate giving us the right to use as much space as we like on fair terms. What a gallant option: You can depend upon it that the syndicate will take this Paris property off our hands only when we take up enough space and pay enough rental to make it a good investment for the syndicate. To do so is equivalent to keeping the property. There is where we have been landed by Sir Henry Thornton. I think the minister should go further and state to this House that the opinion of this House regarding the transaction shall be made known to Sir Henry Thornton by himself. And, further, if as we are told it is the opinion of any legal adviser of the Canadian National
Railway board that this transaction was right I want to assert that, no legal adviser can say it was right, no man with a conscience can say so; he may possibly say it was technically lawful, but it passes my ingenuity to see how he can say even that; but if he or anyone does say it was right-let the government come to this House this session with an amendment that will make such a thing unlawful for all time to come. Do not understand me to suggest that it is necessary, I do not believe it is necessary; the intent and letter of the law is to me as plain as the sun in the heavens. If any general manager who in the responsible position that Sir Henry Thornton is ,'n has no more conception of his duty than to enter into a transaction like that, well, for my part the measure of confidence I have had in him is destroyed.
Will the minister tell us whether headquarters could have been secured in this Paris building without purchasing it, or whether any effort was made to this end?

That is a detail with
which I am not conversant.

Mr. Chairman, if we are to go through this four-hour stunt again for the purpose of giving the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) a chance to express himself, I presume there is no harm in the rest of us who do not pretend to know very much about railway management expressing our opinion on the question. The leader of the Opposition pretends that he is desirous of being fair to Sir Henry Thornton, that he wants to maintain the confidence of the country in the integrity of the Canadian National Railways board. I would remind my hon. friend that the first reception he gave Sir Henry Thornton, before Sir Henry had had an opportunity to get his shoulder in the collar on the job at all, was an attack upon the newly-appointed president of the Canadian National Railways during a by-election in Lanark last fall. So pronounced was this attack that the hon. gentleman's own party press found it necessary to remind him that it was a very unwise proceeding on his part. My right hon. friend will remember what appeared in his own journals.

There was some misinformation given the Journal. I would not
Supply-Railways-C.N.R.

wonder if it was given by the minister himself. I was suspicious at the time that such was the fact. What I stated in Lanark was a perfectly correct statement of the truth, and apparently the electors of Lanark thought so.
I am recalling the incident merely to refresh the hon. gentleman's memory, to remind him that he was not fair to Sir Henry Thornton on that date and has never been fair to him since.
What did I say?

What is he saying now? What is the purpose of his attacks on Sir Henry Thornton? Is it not to destroy the confidence that Sir Henry Thornton himself has won during the time he has been with us? Is it not an attempt to create suspicion in the minds of the public with regard to the administration of this road? In a word, the hon. gentleman is fearful that Sir Henry Thornton is going to make a better job of the management of our National Railways than did his predecessor. That is what is the matter with my right hon. friend.
That is true.

Of couse it is true, [DOT]everybody knows it. I have been watching my right hon. friend's antics in respect to our National Railway system, his solicitous regard for its success; but every time there is any evidence of the system doing better than formerly, well, he is pretty nearly prepared to take some kind of a cat-fit over it. Oh, we know the game of politics, some of us. We do not pretend to be able to play the game very low-down; no, but we can see the kind of people who are playing it.
Let us have a word or two about the propriety of this transaction. We are discussing this expenditure, it is said, after it has been made. Does not that occur constantly in parliamentary practice? Is not every Governor General's warrant expended before it is discussed in this House? Certainly that is so. Unless we can give a certain latitude to the president of this railway system so as to put him on a parity with the president of any other railway system dealing with similar transactions, then we are not going to make a success of our national railways. The president must have some discretionary power or he will not be able to make the system go. If we are going to knock or pull down every day what our president does in the exercise of his discretion, how long are we going to keep a good man in this job? No competent man is going to remain there if he has not the right to use his discretion. The head of every great *organization is given a free hand. He must
{Mr. Meighen.]
be able to exercise his judgment and close out a transaction when it is to the interest of his organization to do so, and afterwards discuss it with his board of directors or his shareholders. In this case the people of Canada are the shareholders. It has not been shown that the accommodation was not required in Paris. The whole discussion has revolved around the question as to whether Sir Henry Thornton had a right to do this thing or not. Well, if he has no right to use his discretion, if he must wait for all the red tape to be cut before he can close out a pi oposition of this kind, then we are not going to make a success of our National Railways, because that principle will be earned all down the line and you will not be able to keep competent and resourceful men in the employ of the National Railway system. I know the technical argument is on the side of my hon. friend, but I take the ground that everybody exercising authority in any position, from Sir Henry Thornton down to the most humble employee, unless he has freedom of action at critical times is going to miss many an opportunity of serving the interests of his organization. This principle applies to government just exactly the same. The man who has to go through all the rigmarole of the red tape, without being allowed to exercise any initiative of his own, would not, it seems to me, be living up to the requirements of a young country like this, which desires, especially at critical times, quick action on the part of its servants.
Would the minister inform the House whether parliament was in session at the time this transaction was under consideration?
I am not discussing whether parliament was in session when the transaction was put through. The Minister of Railways is more familiar with these details than I am.
Parliament was in session.

After getting what we believe to be the best available man on this or any other continent for the management of our National Railway system, are we going to shackle him so that he cannot exercise any initiative, judgment or discretion in matters of this kind? If that is so, we may as well all throw up our hands, because you. cannot run our National Railways in competition with the other big railway system under such an administration.	.
Then the question naturally arises, How much latitude are you going to give the president of your railway system? You will have to depend on his judgment. Why did we

Supply-Railways-C.N.R.
search the four corners of the earth for Sir Henry Thornton if it was not that we could secure a man whose judgment, we could be confident, would be exercised in the best interests of our railway system in just such cases as the one under discussion. I am not entering into the merits or the demerits of this case, I do not know the situation in Paris, and I do not know the requirements of our railway in that respect. Therefore I cannot discuss the merits. I am discussing the wisdom and propriety of giving the head of our National Railway system discretionary power, and I say that unless you give him such power you might as well despair of trying to operate the system successfully.
I have had some experience in handling departments-in a small way, of course, compared with a matter of this kind; and I say that the man who cannot be given discretionary power and who cannot be relied upon as having good judgment should not be left on the job. It is a mighty small piece of business to take the technical attitude that my hon. friend takes, to advertise it all over the country, to try to destroy the confidence of the country in the National Railway system itself and in Sir Henry Thornton. And all this is done under the pretence that it is for the good of the National Railways! No, Mr. Chairman, the first thought of my hon. friend is to make political capital. . Perhaps the Minister of Railways is not without some fault in this matter because of the attitude of the Liberals on a former occasion toward the National Railways. You will remember. Mr. Chairman-you were in the House too -that in 1921 and prior to that, when the question of bringing down information not dissimilar to this was before the House, the Liberals were not sparing of the government of that day, headed by my right hon. friend, in regard to the failure to bring down certain information connected with the National Railways, and in their criticism of Mr. Hanna. But they had this justification, that was a railway board, that was a government, whose passing was long overdue. The Opposition of that day were justified in making the exposures they did in that connection, as subsequent events demonstrated. It is perfectly natural for my hon. friends opposite to retaliate now; I am not objecting to that. I was not here at the time, but I can understand the desire to take advantage of a technical situation like this. I do not ask for quarter on behalf of my colleague at all; let them go to it. But do not imagine that we do not understand the situation. We do understand it, and we will have to see to it that
the country understands it. Hon. gentlemen opposite are trying to square accounts, that is all. Now, we are all desirous of making a success of the Canadian National Railways, are we not? I think we are; I think my right hon. friend, when he forgets politics, if he ever does, is desirous that it should be a success. Why, he is at least the godfather of it himself, if nothing more. And I am sure that most of our Progressive friends are in principle desirous that the National Railways should succeed. Long before the national system was inaugurated they went on record as being friendly to and believing in national railways, and I take it for granted, without discussing it with them at all, that that is their present attitude. I have no doubt that they are ready to forgive much, to overlook much if necessary, in order to give the National Railways a fair trial. Are we not all committed to that idea of giving the system a fair trial? Now, here we have a stranger within our borders. It is true that in Great Britain the railways were operated as a national enterprise, but he has had long experience in connection with the private operation of railways. He has only recently got on the job here-last December-and naturally he will be desirous of using the same discretionary powers that he exercised in the administration of other lines. He recognizes that he has a big competitor; he has to measure up to a high standard, and it is the most natural thing in the world that he should endeavour to make good. All I can say is that if this discretionary power is not to be exercised we cannot keep in our employ the kind of men that we believe Sir Henry Thornton to be; they will not stay with us. As long as I am convinced that he is rightly using this discretionary power and that he is justified in what he does in that connection I am going to stand behind him. because I want to see the national system made the success that I believe it can be made. The development of the next ten years in Canada will be wrapped up with the progress of the Canadian National lines; are we going to jeopardize the success of that development over a matter of this kind? The transaction is not yet completed; it will be time enough to denounce the government or to 'denounce Sir Henry Thornton when we know how this thing ultimately turns out. We believe it will turn out exactly as the Minister of Railways has predicted. If it does, then what difference does it make whether the transaction is done this or that or the other way? The other day we were discussing some question that did not in-
Supply-Railways-C.N.R.

volve anything more serious than whether a member should come in at one door or at the other door; as long as he got in, what was the difference? Time will demonstrate whether or not the exercise of this discretionary power has been overdone; what position are we in to say whether or not it has now been exercised wrongly? If the attitude of the right horn, leader of the Opposition is to be adopted; if, as he says, the head of the railways should have no discretionary authority-all right; good-bye National Railways.
Nobody says it.

Whatever may be said for the advocate that Sir Henry Thornton has on the legality of this transaction, the minister is certainly to be congratulated on the advocate that he has in parliament. The illuminating address of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) had at least this merit: It was not so long as the last one; also it was equally pregnant. His argument is that unless we allow the manager of the National Railways to dig into the treasury without the knowledge of the government or the authority of parliament, you cannot get a manager worth while. I venture to suggest to the Prime Minister, if he is here, that he keep a close watch on the Minister of Agriculture; a minister who pronounces these sentiments and apparently believes them is a very dangerous man to have in charge of funds. There is a measure of discretion, of course, given to all the directors, but it is given in the law, not by ministers on the floor of the House. Apologies do not create an authority. The measure of discretion is fixed there, and it is a very wide discretion; it is a discretion against which we heard bitter complaints in this House two and three years ago. The manager of the National Railways has no more right to flout the law than a clerk in a bank or anybody else-or the Minister of Agriculture.
Where has he flouted the law?
Where has he flouted the law? It is only about two minutes since the minister admitted it.
I did not admit anything of the kind.

The discretion, let me impress on the minister, is fixed in the law, fixed so clearly that no one in the world could honestly evade it or transgress it. It is argued that a manager of a railroad, with a statute which compels him to get the authority of this government for capital investments, can nevertheless go four thousand miles to Paris and plant $2,000,000 of the money of the
fMr. Motherwell.]
people of this country-and that is an exercise of discretion! That is only a technical offence! Similarly, a customs officer who believed there should be a good building in his town for customs purposes would be quite right to take the money in his possession and go out and buy a building; he would only be technically wrong; whether or not he should be censured would depend on how the matter turned out later; and it would be quite proper and worthy of the commendation of the minister in the House provided only that the building had been bought in the name of somebody else. Such is the argument that the government has presented; I do not know how it could be plainer to hon. members. Now, it is the duty of the government to deal with the man who is guilty.
Shall the item carry?
Carried.

It does seem
ridiculous to hear hon. gentlemen say "Carried." I want to say one word to the hon. Minister of Agriculture. If he thinks that by idle threats he is going to prevent proper and legitimate criticism of the board he is wrong. He is not, by what he says, nor is the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) by mysterious statements as to a hidden propaganda going to gag anybody over here. We have always taken the same positional ways. No party is more interested in getting a proper result in connection with the administration of these railways than we are. We believe that that success can only be got if we are able to hold in the management the confidence of parliament and of the people of this country, and we believe that the ordinary citizen of this country, and the ordinary member of parliament, does not like a law breaker. We believe that the ordinary man in the street believes that the sections of the acts of this parliament are not made to be played with or evaded even by the Minister of Agriculture or with his benediction. That is what we think; and we think that if there is one way of ruining this whole undertaking it is by irregularities and illegalities, it is by removing public moneys from the public treasury, it is by making investments which cannot for some time at least-and, I think, for a long time,-be revenue producing while at the same time we have our own people and our own lands without proper railroad facilities. I would have thought that the minister (Mr. Motherwell), if he were actuated by anything except his political bias, would have been just a little anxious for some branch lines that are required

Supply-Railways-C.N.R.
to-day in Saskatchewan and that could have been built with that $2,000,000. But apparently he is quite content that the moneys should be misappropriated and misapplied. The' hon. gentleman has already managed to make one split in his party. I admit he is an authority on the smoke screen. His devious actions in connection with the oleomargarine question, the substitution of bills and the like show what a past master he is. He managed to make a split in his party there, and he is going to make another one here in a minute or two. Why, he gets up, and against the law and against the statutes and against all principles of company administration, he takes a stand diametrically opposed to the stand taken by his colleague the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham). He shakes his head. Did he or did he not commend this action of Sir Henry Thornton? He knows he did. And did not the Minister of Railways just a short few minutes ago apologize for it and suggest that he did not think this transaction or anything of this kind would ever be repeated? Why, the Minister of Railways knows it is all wrong. He has told Sir Henry Thornton that it cannot be done again. He has already dealt with it to the extent of telling Sir Henry Thornton that his action was wrong and that it cannot be repeated. But, of course, my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture takes the opposite view,-it is quite all right that statutes can be broken; it is quite all right that current funds of the country can be switched. Well, I do not know. I hope that the cabinet split will not go any further and that my hon. friend the Minister of Railways will be able to get a little bit of reason across to my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture after the House adjourns. I take it that the law is of consequence notwithstanding anything the Minister of Agriculture has said.
Now my hon. friend the Minister of Railways says there is no suggestion of dishonesty. How can we make any suggestion of dishonesty? Why ought we to make any suggestion of dishonesty? If we were actuated by the motives ascribed to us by the hon. Minister of Agriculture we would say the whole of this is a crooked deal, that is what we would do.
My hon. friend's leader said it was a scandal.
So it is a scandal to break the law. Is it not a scandal for people in high places to pay no regard to statutory obligations of this country? What does my hon. friend say to that?
I say my hon. friend' is making a scandal of it, that is all.

There is nothing that can be made out of this by anybody except what is in it now. But I say that if we were here for the purpose of injuring Sir Henry Thornton we would to-day be saying that there was dishonesty, but we are not. It is an easy thing to say there is dishonesty where you cannot get facts, where you cannot get explanations, where you cannot get figures except one blanket amount, and where you cannot get even the names of the people you are dealing with. The government invited all these charges. We are not making them. We want a success made of the system. We are not making these charges and I ask my friend the Minister of Railways in all seriousness why he would expect us to make a charge of dishonesty? Why did he say that we are not suggesting dishonesty?
The reason I did so-my hon. friend did not make the remark, but one hon. gentleman behind him shouted "Rake-off!"-which would mean dishonesty.

I did not hear it, I did not know anything about that. But I just want to point out this to my hon. friend, that if anyone is injured in connection with the whole of this matter-and I am going to assume the greatest amount of good faith on the part of Sir Henry Thornton until I am shown the contrary-if anybody is injured, if there are charges of rake-offs or that sort of thing made, if the people believe there are secret commissions, that there is something wrong behind all this, who is to blame? My hon. friend and nobody else. He will not give us the information. It well may be that in the absence of information some people will draw certain conclusions. I say, Mr. Chairman, we are unable to get anything that would lead us to any logical conclusion in this matter. We cannot find out, for example, if the syndicate goes through-and my hon. friend hopes it will- how much we are to pay in rent, how big will be the rent guarantee, for what term or anything else. When you do not know any of these things you cannot say one way or the other whether there is indeed a rake-off or not. But I want to point out to my hon. friend that if that impression goes abroad there is no one as much responsible for it as Sir Henry Thornton himself and the government for not giving us the facts.
My hon. friend the Minister of Railways said that other people were trying to get the
Supply-Railways-C.N.R.

property, people we would know about. Now I want to say at once that I do not know anything about anybody else wanting this property or anything about the property. I have not the faintest idea of anybody wanting to get it. I did not know that there was any wild rush at present for real estate in Paris. I did not know that values were advancing by leaps and bounds. I did not know of any wild rush or of any desire on the part of anybody to acquire this property, so, if my friend has any idea of that kind he has it; I have not. I do not suppose, though my hon. friend really knows very much about it. I do not suppose he knows how old the hotel is or whether it is a first-, second- or third-class place. I have been told that once upon a time it was a good place, forty years ago, but that now it is a third-rate place. I do not know anything about it, not in the slightest. I do not know of anyone who was trying to get possession of this property in opposition to and in competition with the Canadian National Railways.
Now, Mr. Chairman, we might just as well be frank about the whole thing. Just see where this matter now stands. We have now got the frank admission of the Minister of Railways-it was a reluctant admission, and it took a long time to get it-that the Canadian National Railways, as a matter of law, could not buy this property. They were not content to stand in a legal position, not content to take the chance of going to the minister-I do not know whether they thought that would be dangerous, that he would turn the proposition down absolutely-they were not content to take the chance of going to the Governor in Council, but devised a scheme whereby the law could be evaded. We have got that admitted. There is no question about it. The Minister of Railways frankly and properly admitted that the Canadian National Railways could not buy that property as a matter of law-there is the admission. And in order to get round the statute, in order to get round the legal position, the name of a clerk is used and the obligation of that clerk is taken. But the money is paid just the same. There is no difference in the real, essential elements of the transaction, not the slightest. The law is broken, public funds are applied in a way in which they cannot be legally applied. And the only man to justify the transaction is the Minister of Agriculture, and I do not think he will, long. My hon. friend who knows about the matter instead of justifying the transaction has reprobated it, and has told the president that this thing cannot happen again. Well, Mr. Chairman, I do not think the matter should rest 
here. The government now know that by a process of manipulation, which has been condemned by the responsible minister, two million dollars of the money of this country has been applied in an illegal investment. What do they propose to do- about it? Are they going to content themselves with just simply warning the president that the law of the country must be observed, or are they going to take steps to see that that money is recovered at the earliest possible date? Are they going to take steps to see that the property is unloaded and the money got back? What do they intend to do? Are they going to do what I have suggested? Or are they going to be parties to rendering it absolutely possible that the whole of this scheme shall be carried out to an easy fulfilment? Are they going to see that such leases are given and such covenants made that anybody will be very glad to take the property off their hands and accept those leases and covenants? They can get rid of the property easily enough if they are willing to pay enough rent, if they are willing to make heavy enough commitments. But what position is to be taken, and what guarantee will the government give that this thing shall not happen again? What is the policy of the government having regard to the rights of the board of directors to denude itself of money on one hand and of property on the other? I repeat, what is their policy? What are they going to do to see that in the future this sort of thing is made entirely impossible? What check will they enforce and what control are they going to take?

I want to take a very few minutes of the committee's time to enter what you might call a protest against the passing of this item, on two grounds. First, I do not believe that we have had sufficient assurance that the service which may be expected from this investment is commensurate with the investment itself; and second, I am quite convinced that there has been a serious irregularity in the purchase. I want to say, first of all, Mr. Chairman, that I do not entertain even the hint of a suspicion as regards the Minister of Railways. I am taking the precaution of saying this because of the outburst of the Minister of Agriculture who-in a long speech, as unconvincing as usual, may I say?-declared that those who are opposing this item are doing it for political reasons. The minister himself was the first, in my opinion, to introduce that phase into the discussion. He made a political attack in which, of course, I am not interested at all. I have no means of entering into the mind of the leader of the Opposition

Supply-R ailways-C .N.R.
(Mr. Meighen) so as to know what prompts him in making his protest, but I imagine if he had any idea to hinder the operations of the National Railways under the present government the best thing he could have done would have been to sit quiet and allow this thing to go unchallenged. Because, if such transactions are allowed as a general principle, I think the downfall of the National Railways is absolutely sure. So that I should say the leader of the Opposition was doing the very best service he could both to this administration and to the National Railways by pointing out the principle that has been violated in this particular regard.
Now, first I say that it has not been shown that sufficient service will be given for the investment made. Two million dollars is quite a lot of money to be invested in a hotel in Paris. It has been advanced by the Minister of Railways that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company have a head office there, and since that is the case he thinks it imperative that the Canadian National Railways should also have a head office in Paris.
My hon. friend asked the question. Did he expect me to say, "No," when I ought to say, "Yes?"
I certainly would not have expected anything of the kind.
I did not refer to the Canadian Pacific Company, it was my hon. friend who did so.

I am quite satisfied with my hon. friend's answer so far as that is concerned. I am trying to get at the justification for this investment and I asked the minister a question. In giving his answer-which is the only answer that has been given to that phase of the question-he stated that the reason for the purchase of this hotel, which is to be used partly as headquarters for the Canadian National Railways, is that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company have headquarters in Paris. But the Canadian Pacific Railway Company are in an entirely different position from the Canadian National Railways. They have steamship lines crossing all oceans, and therefore' it is necessary for that company to have such headquarters in Paris. Let me put the point this way. I cannot conceive of the Canadian Pacific Railway, as it is managed, getting headquarters in some capital in Europe on the same grounds that the Canadian National Railways are seeking to get headquarters in the capital of Continental Europe. I imagine the former company would require much more solid business reasons for purchasing headquarters at a cost of $2,000,000 than have been advanced by the minister in this instance. So I want to register my humble protest. I do not think the investment is a good one. My ideas of an investment, of course, are not worth very much, nevertheless I would expect the minister to give us some more substantial reasons than he has yet given, demonstrating that the investment is worth while from the point of view of service in connection with the Canadian National Railways.
The irregularity of the transaction has been very ably and convincingly set forth. While I am not a lawyer, yet I certainly was able to follow the reasoning, and I am able to say that it has not been answered, nor has any attempt been made to answer it. The best answer that was given, in my opinion, was presented by the Minister of Railways, when he said that the time element entered into it, that it was justified on that ground and that somebody might have "got wise" that the Canadian National was thinking of making this purchase and transfer, and that, therefore, it was necessary to do it speedily. Suppose we look at it from that point of view, I submit that it were better for the Canadian National to even miss what might be a good deal than to break a principle, the breaking of which might spoil it ultimately. It has not been shown that the enterprise itself is a good one. It has not been shown that the investment is sound, nor that the service would come to the national railways by this purchase. Therefore, with all these things in doubt, I think it were better that the legal principle involved should not have been violated. The right hon. leader of the Opposition has made a suggestion-at least I took it as a suggestion-that, since the hon. Minister of Railways has admitted so far that there was some slight error or irregularity, and has stated, that he does not think the like will ever occur again, the opinion of parliament on this matter should be conveyed quietly to Sir Henry. I think that is one suggestion of value.
I should like to ask if it is absolutely impossible for us to get away from this thing in any other way? Must it go on? Must this money be voted? Must the deal be made? Can it not be arrested? If it cannot, will the minister admit that a mistake has been made? There is an honour in admitting a mistake. I would rather vote $2,000,000 to the care of a minister who has the courage to admit that a mistake has been .made, and that he will safeguard the country against the possibility of a recurrence of the mistake, than simply to blindly vote the $2,000,000, without the assurance that this thing will

not recur. I suggest that the minister would frankly admit to us that this was a mistake, a violation of principle, with which he does not concur, and that, the deal having been made, we have to vote the money and it must be paid, but that he will guarantee that, in so far as he is concerned, it will never recur.

My hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) a moment ago mentioned the fact that we were sitting now in the same position as shareholders at an annual meeting, considering the action of its executive. I think it was rather a happy thought, and perhaps one of the most intelligent observations made by him during the course of his remarks. We are in the position of shareholders. I was quite at a loss as a matter of fact, to understand why, however, it was so wholly wrong for shareholders to even question the action of the executive, as my hon. friend upbraided my right hon. leader and others for doing.
In reply to what the minister said a few moments ago when he repeatedly cited the Canadian Pacific and other large corporations in defence of the action of Sir Henry Thornton, namely that the directorate and president have wide latitude in matters of this kind, I said last night, and I repeat now, that the Canadian Pacific shareholders, if they were called upon to put up an additional $73,000,000, and if there were no dividends at all being paid, would very carefully scrutinize an expenditure of $2,000,000 in France on the part of its executive, and I think *would condemn the executive very harshly for making such an expenditure without previously consulting with them. There is no parallel between a corporation operating in a successful manner and paying a dividend, and an institution that is calling upon its shareholders to supplement its losses with votes of new capital. That is on the question of principle or of practice, and altogether aside from the legality of the question. My hon. friend for Calgary East (Mr. Irvine), and other hon. members have asked, can we retire from this proposition? The minister told us the money has been paid and the property purchased, therefore there is no retiring from it. The only recourse we have, or hope to have in the future, is from this mythical syndicate in New York, or supposed to be in New York, whose personnel the minister does not know, unless he has learned it since last week-and I think he should have ascertained the personnel of this syndicate, whose financial standing he does not. know. That is the only possible hope we have. But then we are told

that there is another part of this whole matter that has not been discussed at all. This merely buys the old building which is an hotel. We are told that it is going to be transformed into an office establishment in the centre of Paris, and it is going to be rigged up with a picture theatre, or something of that character, for the purpose of showing views of Canadian life, which is perhaps all right. But that is going to cost the minister some money. I have heard-and again the minister will tell us nothing-that it is going to cost over $600,000, in addition to the $2,000,000, to equip the building. Who is ging to put up that money? Is the national railway going to do it? Is Sir Henry Thornton going to do it? Or is this government going to do it? Who is going to put up the additional sum of money? The worst feature of this whole business is this, that we enter into a discussion with this mythical syndicate as to a rental space in that building, and that our hands are absolutely tied, without any hope at all of having that syndicate complete its deal, unless we gave them a fixed rental for a long period of years-a rental that will ensure them absolutely a profitable return on their investment. The minister said last night that there were no documents and no definite agreement,-nothing in writing. He said that no discussion of the amount of rental had been entered into yet, and not even a verbal understanding. Yet $2,000,000 has been paid over and is in the hands of the purchasers of this property. It is paid out absolutely, and it is our money. Having done all that, we go to the alleged syndicate to fix a bargain for the rental we are to pay for, Heaven knows how long in the future. If I know New York financiers-that is the type that are able to finance-I rather imagine they will be sharp enough to say to this government or to Sir Henry Thornton, "You pay us a rental that will give us about 10 per cent for a great many years-20 years, say-before we will enter into this contract to return you the money." They have not got the money now. That is clear, because Sir Henry Thornton had to put it up. Sir Henry Thornton dipped into the treasury of the country illegally and put it up. Of that there is no question. I move an amendment, seconded by Mr. Boys, as follows:
That item 139 stand until the president of the National Railways submit to the House full information regarding the purchase of certain property in Paris:
(a)	The names and financial standing of alleged syndicate.
(b)	The rate of the rental to be paid.
