(c)	The commission, if any, and to whom paid.
(d)	The reasons why the property was bought indirectly and not directly by the railway company and without any written agreement of any kind whatsoever.
That is information, that, ordinary common sense demands, should be submitted to this committee before it grants $73,000,000 for the president of the National Railways to play with for the next year. What does this item say? Has the committee taken the trouble to note it particularly? This item is virtually granting a blank cheque for $73,000,000, subject to certain conditions. It outlines the manner in which the money is to be paid, and then on the second page this will be noted:
The amount herein authorized may be applied from time to time, in the discretion of the Governor in Council.
And I want the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) to listen to this. He said that this should be spent in the discretion of Sir Henry Thornton; that Sir Henry Thornton should have the discretion to spend this how he liked, and that he was to be brought to book only at some future date and only if he made a mess of the matter. But the law says and the appropriation says this year, as they said last year, that this money is granted, the Governor in Council saddled with the authority or the discretionary power of seeing that it is properly applied. In this case-and I would cite this to support my resolution-the Minister of Railways told us last night that Sir Henry Thornton did not report this transaction to him until after it was done. The Governor in Council had thus no opportunity to exercise discretionary power; the hands of the Governor in Council were tied. I will venture to say that if one could look into the mind of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) at this moment, one would see reflected there the rather heated discussions which occurred in the council chamber within the last few weeks when this transaction became known to the cabinet. Not one of them outside of the burlesque by the Minister of Agriculture, not even the Minister of Railways himself, has attempted to support this transaction this afternoon. The Minister of Railways told us last night that he would have done this in a different way. He told us to-day that he had to apologize to the committee for the transaction, and I do not blame him. I feel that if the minister would be perfectly frank with the committee, he would tell us that he was surprised and mortified when he learned in the first place that this transaction was made; that he had called Sir Henry Thornton into his office and severely reprimanded him for taking this course. I have no doubt that he did so. Why not publicly discipline this gentleman by frankly admitting this before parliament? That will probably do him a great deal of good. Let me put this to the government, and particularly to the Prime Minister. If this transaction had been allowed to pass without comment last night or through this parliament, I venture to say that next year Sir Henry Thornton would not have stopped at $2,000,000 in Paris. The one thing that will prevent this gentleman from repeating this practice is just what has gone on last night and to-day. If a private corporation were concerned, what would prevent him would be the criticism of the shareholders. I want to say to the Minister of Agriculture who lectured us here pretty severely, who charged us with trying to discredit the National Railways, that he cannot discredit the National Railways more effectively than by giving a free hand for transactions of this sort. I want to say to him further that he stands to-day before this country a minister of the Crown knowing this transaction, condoning the move and the steps taken by Sir Henry Thornton; he stands approving the paying over of $2,000,000 of the money of the Canadian people for a mythical and undisclosed syndicate. And he cannot escape that. He has approved it and condoned on the floor of this House. He has approved it and has condemned those who dare to question it. The Minister of Agriculture cannot get away with that sort of thing.- I know his colleagues at least feel and feel keenly-one has only to look at their faces-that this is a transaction that is not to the credit of any government. I have watched each minister yesterday evening and this afternoon, and not one of them is comfortable under this matter. It is to their credit that they are not comfortable. The one thing, however, that is not to their credit is the extent to which they condone this transaction.
An attempt was made yesterday by one of them, the Acting Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) to take responsibility and defend this action. To that extent I think he is culpable together with 5 p.m. the president of the National Railways. This is not a trivial matter; this is not a matter of a small purchase; this is a heavy investment. And we in Canada are striving under a load of debt. One of the difficulties we are faced with is the cost of transportation. What is the problem in the prairie provinces to-day? To get the products of the soil out to the seaboard. What is the chief part of that problem? The cost

of moving that stuff. What makes the cost of moving goods to the seaboard? The cost of operating the railways. Here we have as an exhibition of what we are to hope for in the future in the way of economy in transportation, the president of the National Railways, lightly, flippantly and in a most frivolous manner, flinging $2,000,000 into the heart of Paris, as if that were nothing. What hope is there in this country for economy in operation with an extravagant person like that at the head of the National Railways? Just as soon as possible the president of the National Railways must be brought to understand that that form of extravagance will not be tolerated in this country.
I move this resolution for this purpose, that the members of this House, as shareholders of this great undertaking, mgy receive the information to which we are entitled. The minister has not even been entrusted with the names of the syndicate. Is that appalling fact clear to the House? Think of it! He said at the commencement of the argument last night-and it was an argument-that it was not in the interest of the National Railways to disclose the syndicate. Later on, in reply to a question by myself, he admitted that he did not know the syndicate, and that is the real reason why he cannot disclose it.
Not at all.

He certainly cannot disclose that which he does not himself know. Does the minister know the names of the members of this syndicate? Will the minister answer me that question before I proceed further?
My hon. friend is making an argument and giving a reason why I did not give the names. That is the thing to which I object.
Will my hon. friend be good enough to answer my question: Does he know the names of the syndicate?
I am not in the witness box. My hon. friend has taken the opportunity to ask me a question. I will answer it in my own way and not be dictated to at all.
I am not desirous of dictating.
I have the floor and I am trying to answer the question.
My hon. friend cannot accuse me of being discourteous to him.

I am not doing so. My hon. friend had better let me answer the question. He gave as a reason why I did not give him the names of the syndicate that I

did not know. It is true I do not know; but if I did know, I would be in the same position.
On the advice of the president of the board and with the concurrence, I think, of the solicitor, it is not in the interests of the Canadian National Railways that the details of this unfinished transaction should be made public at the present time.

Very good. Then we
have the minister coming before parliament advising that he, or the government, or the National Railways, has parted with $2,000,000 in the interests of a syndicate whose names not even the minister knows in confidence. This is an appalling situation.

It would be if it were
true.

My hon. friend told us
last night that he did not know the names of the syndicate, and he says he does not know them now. I say it is an appalling situation.

hon. friend said was an appalling situation.
I say that is an appalling situation.
That is his opinion.

Certainly, it is my opinion. The minister does not know the names of this syndicate, that, I think, is the most extraordinary feature about this whole transaction. And yet we are really asked to approve the turning over of $2,000,000 to undisclosed, unnamed and unknown Americans in New York. That is what it amounts to. That is the situation which we cannot excuse, it is a situation that the government cannot defend, and my resolution asks that the names of these gentlemen and their financial standing and ability to carry through this deal be disclosed to the House, so we may know something about who they are, the terms of the rental and the rates to be paid for the space, the lease for which will have to be signed before this House meets again probably tying us up for ten or twenty years, for certainly we ought to have a long-term lease on the main street of Paris-and furthermore, that the reasons why this property to the value of $2,000,000 was bought through an official of the railway company in Paris and not directly by the railway company itself, and why the title should be in the name of this official. This information and these reasons we are entitled to have and they should be given to the committee. My

resolution asks that the committee order that the item stand until this information is brought before us.

I am of opinion that this motion is out of order, for the reasons set forth in Beauchesne at paragraph 169:
A proposed resolution may be allowed to stand over *with general consent until another occasion, but if it has been regularly proposed from the Chair and discussed, no motion for its postponement is regular because there is no period to which it can be postponed.
There is a reference to Bourinot, page 426, which is a repetition of the words contained here, and also to May, page 479, which also stipulates to the same effect, namely:
No amendment can be moved which is not relevant to the grant under consideration, nor can a motion for postponing a proposed resolution be entertained.
Therefore I have to declare this motion to be out of order.

Before you declare it out of order, Mr. Chairman, I shall have something to say about it. I have the greatest admiration for the Deputy Clerk and for his book, but if it says what the Chair states is the law I shall be surprised. The Chair has ruled that a motion to pass an estimate cannot be postponed. Why, such motions have been postponed dozens of times.
By consent.

No, not by consent. You cannot enforce the closure, Rule 17B, without postponing the item under discussion at the time. Under this rule, in order that the closure may apply on the second day, on the first day there must be a motion in committee to postpone consideration of the item. We have moved it over and over again; if I remember rightly before there was any closure rule. The rule that there cannot be a postponement of an item under consideration of the committee is, I think, with all deference to the Chair, preposterous. Certainly there can be a postponement, and we can surely give reasons for the postponement in the body of the motion.	*
The rule I have cited applies only to Committee of Supply according to Bourinot.
Bourinot was written before this rule 17B was passed.
There is another point, that the committee has'no authority to impose a condition upon the House.
We are not imposing a condition upon the House, but upon the committee.
The words of the resolution are, "until the president of the National Railways submit to the House."

That may be. That is not a condition imposed on the House, but a condition that must be fulfilled before this estimate is proceeded with. We cannot restrict the prerogative of parliament, everyone admits that, but to suggest that in Committee of Supply we cannot move postponement of an item does not admit of argument. Let me read section 17B:
Immediately before the Order of the Day for resuming an adjourned debate is called, or if the House be in Committee of the Whole, or of Supply, or of Ways and Means, any Minister of the Crown, who, standing in his place, shall have given notice at a previous sitting of his intention so to do, may move that the debate shall not be further adjourned, or that the further consideration of any resolution or resolutions, clause or clauses, section or sections, preamble or preambles, title or titles, shall be the first business of the committee, and shall not further be postponed; -
"Shall not be postponed."

Certainly, but he has to give notice before. The procedure is this: In Committee of Supply a motion is made that the consideration of the items one by one be deferred, then at the close another motion is made after a day's notice that those deferred items be at the next sitting of the committee the first business 'and that their consideration be not any further postponed. I think I should know the rule pretty well.

I understand my hon.
friend had something to do with the drafting of it,

I did, I had everything to do with it, and I have never had reason to believe it was faulty. I notice that hon. gentlemen opposite who criticized it do not repeal it; they are careful to preserve it. I say that under the closure rule a motion to postpone must be made.
After notice.
No, no.
Read the rule.

The notice is in this form: A motion to postpone is made; there is nothing prior to that; but after that is done, then notice, is given, effective the next day,

that these items, consideration of which has been postponed, be the first business of the *committee and be not further postponed. That is the notice. But the notice is given after. There is a preliminary motion to postpone consideration. There is no question about it at all, and I am sure if the Deputy Clerk has a moment to look it up he will immediately concur with me. The first thing done is a motion to postpone, subsequently there is a notice that at the next sitting of the committee there will be a motion made that all the postponed items be the first business of the committee and be not further postponed. I think, as well, reasons can be given, but I do not speak so definitely on that point. I do not know why reasons should not be given, so long as those reasons are applicable only to the committee. But as to the first there is no doubt whatever.

I do not wish to appeal. I ask that the Chair reconsider the decision, because there cannot be any question about it It is a very serious ruling.

I am occupying the Chair only temporarily, but Rule 169 is very plain to me. It says:
A proposed resolution may be allowed to stand over with general consent until another occasion, but if it has been regularly proposed from the Chair and discussed, no motion for its postponement is regular because there is no period to which it can be postponed.
That is based on Bourinot, and it has been the invariable procedure in Committee of Supply.
That was long before Rule 17B was passed; consequently it must merge into 17B so far as it prevents a motion being postponed.
Closure cannot apply here, because no notice has been given.
I am not asking that it apply. But after that rule is passed there must be eligibility for a motion to postpone. A ruling that it cannot be done means that 17B never can be applied again.

The closure rule, 17B, is in the nature of an exception; it does not

do away with the general rules of the House as they stood before. Now, let us read 17B. It does not state that there must have been a previous motion to postpone; it simplj' says:
Immediately before the Order of 'the Day for resuming an adjourned debate is called, or if the House be in Committee of the Whole, or of Supply, or of Ways and Means, any minister of the Crown who, standing in his place, shall have given notice at a previous sitting of his intention so to do, may move that the debate shall not be further adjourned.
A minister of the Crown gives notice that at the next sitting he will move that a debate be not further adjourned, but there is no previous motion to postpone. The rule does not mention any such motion.

In that case there must have been a previous motion to adjourn, because you could not move that it be not further adjourned unless it has been adjourned once. Similarly, when it is in committee there must have been a previous motion to postpone, otherwise you could not move that it be not further postponed.

For instance, last night this item was discussed and then it was allowed to stand. But if it had not been allowed to stand, the committee would have reported progress; we would sit again to-day and the committee would make the same report. Closure would mean that on a subsequent day the minister would rise and say that when this item would be discussed there would be no further postponement. That is what closure means.

Certainly, that is what closure means. Closure proceeds on the assumption that when a minister says "stand," that is a motion for postponement. When a minister brings in an item he is supposed to move a resolution for the passing of that item. He does not in so many words do so, but as a matter of fact in all application of the closure, in so many words he does so. The closure rule cannot be operated unless on the assumption that there has been a previous motion to postpone, whether in committee or in the House. I am sure the hon. member will come to that conclusion.

Even assuming the right hon. gentleman is right, which I do not admit, I say again that 17B is in the nature of an exception. Secondly it is a rule which applies only in favour of a minister, and the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens') is not a minister. Therefore the old rule, the general rule of the House which has been quoted by the Chairman, should prevail.

I have no intention of appealing against your ruling, Mr. Chairman, not that I wish to agree with it because I think it is perhaps not quite in accord with the rule. The object of this resolution may as well be understood. The object is to have parliament express a vote of want of confidence in Sir Henry Thornton. That is the object of it, no matter how it is brought in or how it is worked out, and the result can only be, if Sir Henry Thornton is

a red-blooded man as I believe him to be, injury which we cannot perhaps estimate to-day to the Canadian National system. I am not going to say that that is the object, because I have no right to say so. I am saying that that may be the result, and every man in this House who votes to haul Sir Henry Thornton, the head of the Canadian National Railways, before us to give certain information which through me he has said to this House will be detrimental to the Canadian National System, votes want of confidence in the head of that system. Sir Henry Thornton has made a success of the system up to date and is making a success of it to-day, and if everything hon. gentlemen said were true the members of this House must understand that they are taking the responsibility of leaving the Canadian National railway probably without a head in the midst of a busy traffic. What the object is I do not know, but the result may be that, and the men who pretend to be in favour of making a success of the national railways cannot well vote, even if what my hon. friend has said is true, want of confidence in a man who up to date is making a success of that great undertaking, which is the greatest experiment in government ownership and operation that we have had in the Dominion of Canada.
I knew something would come up to give an opportunity to divide this House. The Liberal party, even those who do not believe in public ownership, are obliged to give it a fair trial. Not that every one of us believes in it. I know many do not, but we are pledged to give it a fair trial. Hon. gentlemen over there are pledged to government ownership, and now we have a distinct cleavage between the men who are trying to destroy public ownership and the men who are in favour of it. My hon. friend can disguise it anyway he likes. I have given the opinion of Sir Henry Thornton as head of the railway, an opinion that will be shared by every business man, that an uncompleted transaction of a great corporation should not be divulged to the shareholders even though the shareholders be the Parliament of Canada. My hon. friend took the same ground in his term of office, that to divulge an uncompleted transaction might be detrimental to the transaction. He asks for the name of a syndicate in New York. To give that would be to give him half the information that Sir Henry Thornton thinks would be detrimental to the system. What would happen when the representative of this syndicate in New York landed in Paris later on to make ar-

rangements as to the rentals? The Old Country system of rentals is different from ours; they have leases that run for years and are very valuable, and whoever takes over this property has to take over these leases and make some settlement with the leaseholders. And we are asked to announce to every person in the world that we are taking over this property and let the leaseholders be prepared to make the biggest bargain they can possibly make. If it was a private concern such information would not be asked for. They would take the word of those responsible. Acting as the go-between between the government and the president of the Canadian National Railways I have been advised by Sir Henry Thornton that in the interests of the Canadian National system it would not be well, for obvious reasons, to give the particulars of this arrangement about to be completed. That being the case I want to warn hon. gentlemen about the specious argument of getting Sir Henry Thornton here. That argument, no matter how specious it is, if backed up could only have the result of injuring the system and making public ownership possibly a failure in the Dominion of Canada.

My hon. friend has made a very gallant effort to divert the attention of the committee and of the country from this transaction, which he does not attempt now to defend, to the great question of dividing the country and the House upon government ownership of the railways. He does not need to reach very far in any direction from where he is sitting to touch those who attack the government ownership of railways. As far as I am concerned, and I think I can speak for many others here, we are anxious to see this government ownership of railways succeed. But we are not prepared to give unrestrained liberty to any individual who apparently is inclined at least, if not to abuse that liberty, to treat it in a very trivial manner. My hon. friend asks what is going to happen if the name of this syndicate is disclosed. When they go to Paris it will be known that some syndicate representing the Canadian National Railways is going to do some business there. Why, Mr. Chairman, it was placed before this country in the press two weeks ago that Sir Henry Thornton had bought a hotel in the heart of Paris, and that he was going to transform the whole building into offices for the Canadian National Railways and to house the High Commissioner and other departments. All these details were disclosed two weeks ago, and
234 i
everybody in Paris that is interested, everybody in the world that is interested, knows all that the minister says this resolution of mine is going to disclose to the world. Such an argument is not worthy of the long parliamentary experience and intelligence of the minister.
My hon. friend will not fool anybody with that.
Possibly, but the minister will never fool anybody with the argument he made about interfering with the business of closing out certain leases.

Might I ask the hon. member a question? When he was trying to get a lease of Point Grey sand heads out at Vancouver, why did he not come out and tell the people who were behind the transaction and give the public the name of the company?

That is pretty nearly as good a herring drawn across the trail as the minister attempted to draw. Sand was being taken from what was alleged to be government property at the time, and the Public Works department at Ottawa imposed a restriction upon it. However, that has nothing to do with this matter.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: It is a good illustration.

Inasmuch as the committee seem to desire the facts I can give them and very quickly. The facts of the case are these: There are certain sand heads off what is known as Point Grey just at the mouth or entrance to Vancouver harbour. These sand heads were claimed by the Public Works department of Canada for the right of the Dominion, they were also claimed by the provincial authorities. Certain persons dealing in sand, lime and gravel were taking the sand off these sand heads. Other persons made application for what is known as a license or a lease, which is a common form. granted by the Public Works department to take sand from these banks. This application was entertained by the Public Works department and granted. The provincial authorities disputed it. The matter was carried to the Privy Council, and it was decided that the title to the property rested in the province, and the parties who got the license from the Dominion authorities were out of pocket whatever investment they had

made. That is all there is to it. Now, Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to digress into matters of this kind.
Another smoke screen.

Yes, another smoke screen. I want to say to the minister that the information we are asking for is reasonable information. It is not unreasonable, it is not information calculated to interfere with the National Railways. We are not asking that Sir Henry Thornton be brought to the bar of the House, or before any committee. We are simply asking, in view of the admitted ignorance of the minister of the facts, that this item should stand until these facts, which are facts I think the committee are entitled to, are disclosed.

I think a good many members in this House, more especially members in this quarter of the chamber, have listened to this long and protracted debate that lasted all yesterday afternoon and evening, and apparently it is going to last all this afternoon-
Only last night, not yesterday afternoon.

Very well, it does not make
very much difference. I do not like to act in the role of a critic but really it surprises me to hear the nature of speech after speech made here. It is simply a case of member after member getting up and repeating what previous members have said. I have been really anxious for information in order to know just how to form an opinion on this matter, and I was quite prepared to listen, I think without prejudice, to either side in order to get at the foundation of this whole affair. At the very commencement it did strike me that it was rather a serious thing. We are very anxious for the success of the National Railways. I think, perhaps, all of us are, with probably a few exceptions. We have a man at the head of affairs and apparently accusations are being cast at him from the House here of having been injudicious, of having overstepped the bounds of prudence-in fact doing what was really illegal. The accusations may or may not be true. Perhaps I have not a legal mind, a judicial mind. I am not just prepared yet to express an opinion as to *exactly how far the president over-stepped what it was his right to do. Nevertheless, I cannot help but think, Mr. Chairman, that the desire to manufacture a certain amount of political ammunition is entering into this debate, and there has not been an earnest desire, perhaps, to give that information to the

House that it is in the power of some members to give. I have not a bit of hesitation in saying that I believe the right hon. the leader of the Opposition probably knows just as1 much about all these matters as do some hon. gentlemen on the front government benches. I may be wrong or I may be right but I have the suspicion that certain hon. members know a great deal more than they are telling, that they are not taking the House into their confidence, that they think they have got the government in a very embarrassing position, and they are going to make the very most of it from a political point of view. That is the inference I have drawn and I am drawing it without being influenced by any prejudice whatever.
It is good drawing.
Yes, for you.

I beg your pardon. If you
would keep in your own seat it would be better.
He is in a bad corner there.
I cannot say that I am entirely satisfied. There is perhaps a little more mystery about the whole of the circumstances than I would like to see in this House.

Why not try to
get at the bottom of it then?

Excuse me. Perhaps you
will be able to enlighten us when you get up; we have not heard from you yet. I take this point of view-I may be right or I may be wrong-there is some mystery here that I would rather not see in connection with this matter. But the consequences are so great, the issues are so tremendous, in regard to the management of these railways, that I am willing to let the matter go at the present time. But if subsequently when information comes to this House it can be shown that the government has acted in any underhand or improper way, that the proper handling of the country's money has been prejudiced in any shape or form, then no man in this House will be more ready to condemn them than I am. But taking all the circumstances into consideration at the present time I do not believe it is in the public interest that this matter should be debated at any further length. I believe that incalculable harm has already been done by this debate...
Purposely.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think this
is, perhaps, an opportune moment to say a word as to the relations between the government and the Canadian National Railways, and particularly as to the relationship between Sir Henry Thornton, as the head of the railways, and myself in the position which I occupy at the moment. When the government asked Sir Henry Thornton to take control of the railroad we gave him- and I in the name of the government gave him-a distinct pledge that he would be entrusted with the management, that he would have a board of directors with whom he would be associated, and that the board and he as president would be given a free hand, and that there would be no interference on the part of the government with the action which they were taking. We told him, however, that we would hold him responsible for the manner in which he conducted the affairs of the system, but that while we held him responsible we would give him a free hand and would not interfere with him.
That was one possible attitude. The other attitude would have been that as a government we would wish to know everything that he was doing, and the responsibility then would be ours. Sir Henry Thornton in his first interview with me made it perfectly clear that unless he and the board of directors were to have a free hand in the management of that road he would not. for one minute consider accepting the position of president. From the moment Sir Henry Thornton took over the control of the railroads to this hour there has been no attempt on the part of the government, in any particular, to influence his judgment or his course of action in any matter. Whether there will be reason in the future to alter the attitude that we have assumed towards him and the board of directors will depend very largely upon how different transactions of the road turn out in the course of affairs.
So far as this particular transaction is concerned, the position, as I understand it, that Sir Henry Thornton takes, is that to-day there is known throughout Europe one great railway system in Canada, the Canadian Pacific Railway; that the people of Europe know nothing whatever about the Canadian National Railways; that if Canada is to get her share of business from Europe for her
system of railways she must be as much on the map in the heart of that continent as the Canadian Pacific Railway is and have as wide a connection not only with the railroads on this continent but with the railroads in Europe so as to get the benefit of any business in the way of traffic originating there. Sir Henry Thornton, in his judgment felt it desirable for the Canadian National Railways to obtain a site in the heart of Paris which would be conspicuous, and where the affairs of the railway might be so put before the European public that they would soon become conscious that there was a competitor to the other great transcontinental railway system in Canada, namely the Canadian National Railways.
Sir Henry Thornton, like every other railway president, in endeavouring to carry out a move of the kind, naturally surrounded his actions with a certain degree of secrecy. He took this action without any knowledge on the part of the government. Nothing was said to the government with respect to what he or the board of directors proposed to do. Why? Because we told him we expected him and not the government to manage the railway. Does the House wish us to change that policy? Does the House ask us to go to Sir Henry Thornton and say "From now on you shall not enter into any business transaction without placing it before the government and having us approve of it?" If that is the attitude hon. members want us to take, we shall have to change our whole policy with respect to giving a free hand to the Canadian National and giving the board of directors a chance to manage it as in their judgment they think best.
Sir Henry Thornton felt it necessary there should be a building in a conspicuous part of Paris which would be known as the Canadian National headquarters. I have no doubt that, in his endeavour to get the best building, he was anxious to make it in every way the centre or home of Canadian business, and possibly he has had in his mind the moving of our Canadian offices into that building, and perhaps getting other business interests in Canada to rent premises as well. It is a business matter. As a man of wide business experience, he probably knows what is best to do in a transaction of this kind. If Sir Henry has seen fit. to conduct that transaction as all business houses transact their business, with a certain amount of secrecy, I think we all owe it to him to wait and see how his experiment works out before we pronounce judgment upon it; and so far as
Supply-Railways-C.N.R.

the government is concerned I wish to say that we stand here prepared to support Sir Henry Thornton in the transaction which he has made and the step which he has taken. We will judge him as the head of the railway by the manner in which that particular transaction, as well as all other transactions while he is president of the road, turn out. But while he is president of the Canadian National, and we are representing the people of Canada in this House we propose to give Sir Henry Thornton in this and every other transaction precisely the same degree of latitude and freedom as the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific would give to Mr. Beatty.

I shall not adopt the pose of sitting in judgment upon any individual or any part in this House. I listened with a great deal of care to the discussion last night, and I read the debate in this morning's Hansard, with a view of ascertaining the facts in connection with this particular matter. At the outset I may say that I yield to no man in the House in my desire to see the Canadian National Railway experiment prove a splendid success. I say further that I have every confidence in Sir Henry Thornton as an experienced railway man. While I know little about it, I am prepared to give him the heartiest possible support that it is possible for one in my humble position to give. I think the government, in assuming the attitude which was assumed towards Sir Henry, acted properly. They gave him a free hand to administer and manage that particular railway. I think it was desirable to do that, because, of course, it was a matter of tremendous moment to the country, a matter fraught with a great deal of significance to the people of Canada. But I suggest to the Prime Minister that the free hand was given to Sir Henry subject to the laws of this country. Even the Prime Minister of the country is not in a position to override the law. That is a matter for parliament.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Where has the law been overridden?

I think perhaps the fact that the Prime Minister was not in attendance in the House earlier, and did not hear the frank admission of the Minister of Railways, would justify him in asking the question.
The question I asked has not been answered.
I will deal with the Minister of Agriculture in a moment.
I should like to hear from the hon. member wherein the transaction was unlawful.

Perhaps the hon. senior member for Halifax has not been in the House either. I am not going to say anything further except that I commend the Minister of Railways for coming before the House and saying that in his judgment it was improperly done.

I wish I had had a legal training. I could then express things much better than I do express them. Our legal friends, when they get up, kind of put you "in wrong" with their language and not your own. I distinctly said if I had been doing it that I would probably not have done it in the way it has been done. I also said that the solicitor for Sir Henry Thornton informed Sir Henry that the transaction was perfectly legal, and that I stood by his opinion rather than by the opinion of others.

It is not my purpose in view of the discussion that has taken place to argue as to the legality or illegality of the transaction. Suffice it to say that I simply expressed my opinion, after a fairly close examination of the statutes in this regard, that the transaction so far as it has gone is illegal. I do not say it is improper. I impute no motive of impropriety to Sir Henry Thornton at all.
Under what clause of the act does the hon. member undertake to say that the transaction is unlawful or illegal?

If the hon. member will look at the Canadian National Railway Act, and refer to sections 11 and 23, he will find that the powers given to the officers, the president and the board of directors, are there enunciated. That is the limit of their power. I have sought in my own mind some justification for the expenditure in Paris, and so far as I can observe, about the only justification so far urged has been that apparently the Canadian Pacific Railway has a very ambitious office in that city. They, too, are on the front street of Paris. But I am not so sure that it should always be the ambition of the Canadian National Railways to live in the atmosphere of the Canadian Pacific Railway.
That is where they are today.

Then I think it is unfortunate. If the minister suggests that the Canadian National is living in the atmosphere of the

Supply-Rail ways-C.N.R.
Canadian Pacific I am sure a lot of people will view that statement with a good deal of regret.

We are compelled to admit the fact, not in any theoretical sense that the Canadian Pacific is here. We are confronted with a healthy rivalry and we have to do the things a business firm would do, in order to get our share of the business, if we are going to make a success of the road.

My suggestion was that, so far as I was able to observe, the substantial reason given was to put it in this sense, that the Canadian National must live in the atmosphere of the Canadian Pacific. In this particular transaction, it appears to me that the moneys belonging to the people of Canada, have been taken for the purpose of financing a New York syndicate, in order that they may subsequently at some time purchase this particular property. That I think is an undesirable thing for the Canadian National Railway board to do. I do not think it is a commendable thing that the money should be taken from the coffers of this country in the method indicated and used for the purpose of allowing a New York syndicate to subsequently acquire control of this particular property.
The Minister of Agriculture interrupted just a few moments ago and I want to compare his words in this matter with those of the Minister of Railways. The Minister of Railways says frankly that if he were carrying out this particular transaction, he would not carry it out in this particular manner at all. On the other hand, the Minister of Agriculture, in the light of that fact and with the knowledge imparted to him by the Minister of Railways, seeks to give this transaction his special benediction. I want to dissociate myself from the attitude assumed by the Minister of Agriculture. That I do not believe to be a commendable code of morals whatsoever, and all I can say is that he made a most illogical apology for an illegal act.
The question is: What can be done under the circumstances? The transaction may be and, perhaps, is perfectly legitimate, and I have little doubt that upon investigation, it wall be found that the transaction is in the best interest of this country and of the Canadian National Railways. Why is it not possible for us to get these facts? A few material facts are required, and it seems to me that we have a right to ask for the facts, in view of the expenditure, particularly outside of this country, of something over $2,000,000. I do
not see how anybody could be prejudiced, despite the statement of the Minister of Railways with regard to the leaseholders. The facts are already known; they have been within the knowledge of members for some time, and they must be within the knowledge of the leaseholders of that particular hotel building in Paris. Therefore, I would suggest that, perhaps, the minister would be willing to allow the matter to stand in order that he can get the facts that are required and place them before the House. I am sure neither he nor Sir Henry Thornton will ever regret having stated to the House all the facts.

The difficulty with that is that my hon. friend must not forget, as some hon. members seem to be trying to forget, that Sir Henry Thornton is the head of the Canadian National Railways, and responsible for its success to the people of Canada. He knows the situation, and he has told me that to divulge the details of this transaction at the present time would be detrimental to the interest of the Canadian National Railways. If I approached him again, he would tell me the same thing. Under those circumstances, if we have any faith in Sir Henry Thornton, we ought to do with him exactly what would be done by the shareholders with the head of any great company-accept his word and act accordingly.

The House resumed.

Will the minister obtain, before we meet at eight o'clock, information as to where the transaction is? How fat has it proceeded? Have we, or has the Canadian National Railways, any contractual relationship yet with this syndicate in New York? How far has the syndicate proceeded? When we know that, we shall know a little better just how to estimate the advice which Sir Henry Thornton gave.
While I am on my feet, I am going to enter a protest against the too oft repeated assumption of the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) that he is sitting in final arbitrament over the moral quality of all other people in this House; nor do I thank him for the suggestion that I have certain information of my own about this transaction which I am concealing from parliament. I should like to know his authority for this suggestion. I tell him I know nothing about this, not one word, not a tittle of information, that he does not know if he has sat through the discussion in this House. I ask h'm. before he attributes to me concealment of facts known to myself for partisan
Supply-Railways-C.N.R.

purposes, that he have some authority for his words. He goes on and he states with an air of sanctimonious complacency, that we of the opposition have no right to proceed with our criticism because we are seeking party advantage. I do not pretend not to be seeking party advantage provided that it is legitimate and right, and I do not expect the leader of the Progressive party to pretend to parliament not to be seeking party advantage provided it is legitimate and right. Am I to be deterred from criticism of a transaction which I believe to be wrong and which I believe I can demonstrate to be wrong, because if we succeed in bringing wrongdoing home to the government, it would be detrimental to an opposing party? Are we continually to be taunted, when we make criticism or censure that we are acting merely in a partisan spirit and not doing our duty as members of parliament? What does he conceive to be our duty?
If my right hon. friend would ask only one question at a time, I would have some chance to remember it.

I proceeded on the
assumption that the hon. member's mind can carry more than he thinks it can. I will put my questions one by one in future.

I had made some references to comments on the motives of members of this House in attacking the transaction in question. I want to refer for a moment to the appeal made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). The Prime Minister seems to think that the question whether we know where we are at in connection with this deal or do not is really a question between political management of the Canadian National Railway and business management. Could a more preposterous suggestion be made? He says, "We told Sir Henry Thornton to go ahead and we would give him a free hand; we would not interfere with him at all." Sir Henry Thornton did as he was told; consequently it cannot be wrong. If the government told Sir Henry Thornton to go ahead beyond what Sir Henry Thornton and his board's powers were under the act, then the government is accountable to this House and should receive just what Sir Henry Thornton is receiving. Sir Henry Thornton is properly told to go ahead with the management and operation of the railway, and I would that the government were carrying out to the full the whole spirit and intent of the injunction they gave him so far as management and operation go. But the government has no right to tell Sir Henry Thornton to go ahead and invest moneys of this country in capital ventures unless parliament has previously voted the money to do it. The Minister of Railways definitely told us they did not tell him to go and do that; that they gave him no authority at all; that he never consulted them in any way. Consequently he is clearly subject to reprimand, and no one would be doing his duty in par-

Supply-R ail ways-C .N.R.
liament if be did not make that perfectly manifest.
Now, the question is this: Should we vote the $73,000,000 that is before us, which is the main railway vote to the National Railway board, until we know what position the country is in? I come in this connection to say a few words as to the minister's argument. The minister's argument is: Here is an attack on the railway; if we submit to this motion and do not pass this $73,000,000 item without the information demanded, it simply means that the opponents of the National Railway must definitely sever themselves from its supporters and the issue be joined throughout the country. I do not know what the minister means. Is the House not entitled to know where we are at with respect to two million dollars of our money that has gone from our possession? We do not know about it; the minister himself does not know, and all we ore asking is that he find out.
We may be in one of two or three positions. We may be the definite owners of the property, of course, in the name of the National Railways or rather of Aronovici. We may be the final owners of it, and so far as the legal position is concerned, my thought is that that is where we are. So far as I have been able to find from the minister, we have no undertaking of anybody to take it off our hands, we are tied there by the act of Sir Henry Thornton in defiance of the law of Canada. Well, if we are in that position the hour has struck now for a reprimand. We may be in another position: we may be in a position of temporary ownership, legal ownership, with the undertaking of others to take it off our hands at what we paid for it, subject to some understanding on our part that we will help them out by a leasehold interest. If we are in the latter position, which the minister intimates we are in, surely we are entitled to know the facts about it. Surely we are entitled to know the value of the covenant we have, if we have such a covenant, with this syndicate in New York, and if we vote this money, when are we going to know? When we vote this $73,000,000 we place it or authorize the minister to place it month by month where Sir Henry Thornton can do with it again just what he has done now. Should we do that till we know the real position we are in as to the first $2,000,000? Oh, the Prime Minister says, we ought to give him full authority to buy hotels in Paris or buy hotels in Hong Kong, and not only should he have the authority, but if he does it parliament should not know the facts about it.

speechtext:

a little doubtful before.

I am more confirmed.
The Prime Minister did not state to this House that this vote should go through before we know the f&cts as to the late transaction. His Minister of Railways has told us over and over again that we do not know the facts, that he does not know them himself. He does not know who the syndicate are whose credit we are asked to take for this $2,000,000 that has gone. Are those facts to be known or are they not? They are not known. We are told we are not to know them until the $73,000,000 is placed in the position where it may go in exactly the same direction and by the same plan. Now is it an unfair thing to ask of the minister that before he asks parliament to vote $73,000,000 more to be in a position to be used just as Sir Henry Thornton used this, he should be in a position to tell this House what really has happened to the last $2,000,000? He is not to-night.. The reason he gives I must say I do not appreciate. I do not^know what harm it is going to do that syndicate for this parliament and for the government to know who they are. The minister says there are tenants in that building and if they know who own it it wiil be hard, for those owners to make terms with the tenants. How can they make * terms with the tenants until the tenants do know who owns it? I do not see what difference it makes to the
Supply-Railways-C.N.R.

tenants whether it is owned by Aron-ovici in Paris or Moses-ovici in New York. What is the difference to them? If there is any reason for secrecy the minister has not suggested any circumstance that would justify his claim for secrecy, none at all. Certainly the tenants of the building know it has been sold. The minister has told the House that, he has volunteered it himself; it has been in the papers for two weeks. They know it has been sold and that arrangements have to be made, and how is it going to hurt the owner that the owner should be known? But even if it is going to, are not we entitled to know? Why should we vote money without knowing to whom the last money we voted has gone or at whose credit it rests at this hour? That is the position the Opposition takes. There are hon. members of this House who say it is all right-all right that $2,000,000 of the money of Canada, $2,000,000 added to the deficit of Canada on the National Railways should lie somewhere in Paris subject to redemption at the hands of men we do not know anything about, and whose names even the Minister of Railways has no knowledge of. Now if other hon. members are satisfied with that condition I am not, and I do not propose to take the responsibility of voting-further money until we do know. If the House wishes to do it, then my vote will be the measure of the responsibility I take.
The minister says:	Do not attack Sir
Henry Thornton. Look at the success he has made of the National Railways. Well, that question is not up for discussion now. But I venture to say to the minister that the National Railways were succeeding just as well when Sir Henry Thornton took charge as they are to-day, that they were succeeding just as well at the hands of the manager whom he and his government dethroned and cast out of office, certainly as well as they are to-day. I venture to say more, if you will search the whole history of Mr. Hanna's tenure of office you will find nothing to compare with a transaction like this. No, it was never even alleged that he went beyond the limits of his power, never alleged that he broke the confidence of the Commons of this coqntry or went beyond the limits fixed by statute as the limits within which he ought to restrain himself. No, no breach of confidence was ever even suggested of Mr. Hanna. But the question of Sir Henry Thornton as general manager is not the question before this House, and the minister cannot make it so. The question is this, whether in a case where admittedly money has been wrongfully taken from the treasury of the

Canadian National Railway we are not entitled to know just exactly the position that money is in before we vote more money into the same position. That is the only question before us.
The Prime Minister says the money has not illegally gone, and the Minister of Railways says it has not illegally gone. The Minister of Railways admitted that if they had bought the property in their own name it would have been illegal, that they had not the power to do so and we are supposed to be satisified because they went through the formality of putting it in the name of Mr. Aronoviei. The matter is not changed in the slightest by the property being in the name of Mr. Aronoviei. The essential facts are these, that plainly in defiance of the word of parliament and the statute of Canada, $2,000,000 has gone out of the treasury of the Canadian National Railway, and we are supposed to vote more money where it may be similarly dealt with without knowing the position the last $2,000,000 is in.

Mr. Chairman, I might be
permitted to say a few words in reply to the lecture I received from the right hon. leader of the Opposition. Let me say at the outset that I have in no way freed the government from responsibility in this matter. I stated my opinions then. I also ventured to assert that probably the right hon. leader of the Opposition knew just about as much about this transaction as the government. At this statement he was very indignant, and that surprised me very much because I listened to speeches last night and this afternoon by members in that part of the House twitting the government with knowing nothing about this transaction, so I do not see why he should have been so indignant when I insinuated that he probably knew as much as they did. But I am quite *willing to take it back if I am wrong. I onljr made a guess.
The right hon. leader of the Opposition also told me that I had no right to lecture the members of this House. Well, I do not know that he has the keeping of all this House in his pocket. Is he the particular guardian of their rights and privileges? I can hardly see why he should take what I said to himself so very quickly if I was not hitting a sore spot. I have a great deal of respect for the right hon. gentleman, and I think he knows it. I respect his ability, his industry, and his many good qualities, but I want just to tell him right here and now that if he thinks that any special or peculiar sanctity surrounds the personality of the leader of the Opposition

Supply-Railways-C.N.R.
he is entirely mistaken. Now, I think, perhaps I have said enough; but I do not intend to be lectured by the leader of the Opposition, or any other member in this House, when I am occupying a position that I have a perfect right to occupy. I think, Mr. Chairman, you will all acknowledge that since my election to this House I have not indulged in any long speeches; I have never wasted the time of the House. Perhaps in that respect I have made a mistake and allowed opportunities to pass that I ought to have taken advantage of. However I am going io promise hon. members that from this time forward I am going to utilize my due share cf the time which is available for discussion.

I do not wish to keep the House very long, but I am more or less in sympathy with the sentiments that have been expressed concerning the 82,000,000 which is under discussion. It seems to me that the attitude of the government, or of the Minister of Railways, is that we should sign a blank cheque and allow moneys to be spent without asking for details. That is the only interpretation to be placed upon the attitude of the government or of the minister. As to the purpose for which this money is taken we have had no specific details. Am I not therefore justified in saying that we are practically asked to sign a blank cheque? We have a total contemplated expenditure under the vote before the committee of $73,000,000 which may be spent for this, that or the other purpose, and I think we would be establishing a wrong precedent if we voted this money without any question or without criticism. To my mind in this case there is justification for more or less criticism. In private life I could not for a moment think of taking such an attitude as is assumed here in respect of matters of business. I want to say that I have all respect for the Minister of Railways, and if he had been duly advised of all the details concerning this arrangement, or this understanding, and had come to the House and given his word of honour as a gentleman and as a bus'ness man that the arrangement was all right, and also had advised Sir Henry Thornton that such a method of doing business did not meet with his approval, I would be prepared to accept the hon. gentleman's word in that regard. But when no real information is supplied to the committee concerning the matter I am disposed to be more critical than I otherwise would be.
Now, I do not know whether the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) has been disposed of or not but I wish to call the attention of the committee to this circumstance; that some few weeks ago when a very interesting debate took place here on the question of immigration we asked that the item be deferred. I do not think there was a formal resolution but it was asked that the appropriation be deferred and brought down in a more itemized form. That was done and the total was divided into, I think, at least sixteen different items. The request in question was very7 readily apceded to at that time and it seems to me that this demand of the hon. member (Mr. Stevens) is no departure from the principle then admitted. I think that by adopting such a precedent to-day we may reasonably infer that in other cases, let us say for example the Canada Colonization Company, if they are granted an appropriation next year, there will be a repetition of making expenditures in advance of parliamentary authority. That is a wrong precedent to establish, and we have a right to insist that such things should not continue.
The Minister of Agriculture claijned that the West is in favour of government ownership, and he pointed to the fact that that principle had been carried out in the matter of these railways. I think, however, that statement needs a little qualification. As the matter stands in the West we are in favour of the principle of government ownership, and I wish to remind the minister that we predicted fifteen years ago that government ownership would come. However, if the minister will cast his mind back and take the case of the Saskatchewan Co-operative Elevator Company he will realize that the sentiment of the people of the West runs more along the line of co-operation rather than government ownership. Yet we give our hearty support to the principle of government ownership, or more properly speaking public ownership, of railways. That condition has been forced upon us. I have no desire to harass the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite but I would remind them that some years ago we gave a blank cheque to a Liberal government with respect to the Grand Trunk Pacific, the construction of which line they said would not cost the country one cent. That is one reason why vre hesitate to grant any more blank cheques in the case of other arrangements or agreements. The country has not forgotten the experience of the past. Our past experience renders us very cautious in regard to agreements of this kind. Possibly this discussion will serve a very useful purpose if it teaches these men who talk of money in millions and wdio do not have to

*1 am opposed to this vote unless further information is given as to its necessity. The ground of my opposition is that with the information in my possession I think $2,000,000 is an excessive price to pay for this property, if it is the one indicated "in the public press. I saw the Hotel Scribe m 1911, I saw it again in September, 1921, and while I cannot for a moment set myself up as a valuer of property in Paris yet I feel that I can say, with all confidence, that $2,000,000 for that property is a price that has something behind it. It is not even on "the main street," and I appeal to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and to the Minister of Finance, who were in Paris very recently, to confirm that statement. If you take 82,000,000 at 5 per cent that means $100,000, and no one can tell me that the American Express Company, which occupies a corner of the Rue de la Paix near the Place de l'Opera, pays 1,400,000 francs for its yearly tenancy of that building. It does seem to me that before a matter of this kind, coming up in the way in which it does', should be accepted by this House we ought to know that $2,000,000 is a fair price, or anything like a fair price, for the Hotel Scribe. The public prints also tell us that the de facto Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Duncan Marshall, was in Paris recently. I want to say, Mr. Chairman, and I know the responsibility I take in doing so, that I am perfectly satisfied that if any member of this parliament had gone to Paris to bargain for what was known as the Hotel Scribe-I do not know whether it is still occupied as the Hotel Scribe, but it was formerly known by that name-and had $2,000,000 in his pocket the property could have been bought for much less money. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I think there ought to be some means of testing whether an excessive price, a price with a meaning behind it, has not been agreed to be paid for this property.

Before this vote carries I would like to ask the minister if the government have in view any purpose in regard to the Transcontinental railway to Quebec. That road is practically out of commission at
fMr. Gould.]
the present time. I think that in 1919 there were no less than 7,000,000 ties put on it, ties that had not worn out but had rotted from lack of use. I presume that by this time they will have rotted also, and it seems to me that some use ought to be made of that section of the line. Recently a number of us from the west visited the city of Quebec and saw a shipment of cattle from western Canada loaded on board a steamship there. There are a great many advantages in shipping those cattle through the port of Quebec. They arrive there in very much better condition than they arrive at Montreal. The facilities for handling them at that port are so much more superior to the facilities at Montreal that the United Grain Growers, I understand, paid a vessel $600 to stop there. Hon. members can see the situation. The full freight from Montreal to Liverpool was charged, although the cattle were loaded at Quebec. The Grain Growers paid a bonus of $600 to the steamship company for taking these cattle on board at Quebec, and yet they figured that, in the saving of shrinkage and the saving of time, they were money ahead by bringing the cattle over the Transcontinental to the latter port. It appears to me that if a proper grain rate were put into, effect on the Transcontinental a great deal of the overflow, which at present goes down through the United States and which is used to create business for American ports, would go to Quebec.
It seems rather remarkable, and it is discriminatory in fact, that to-day the rates on grain from Port Arthur, or an equivalent point on the Transcontinental, say Armstrong, to Quebec, is just double the rate charged for handling grain for a similar distance in the West, and one might be almost pardoned for supposing that those in charge of the operations of the railway were discriminating against that port, in favour of either the American route or the lake route. I know that some hon. members in this House are of the opinion that under the prevailing grain rates in the West, the Crowsnest pass rates, the railways are losing money in handling our grain. If any hon. member will look over the statements of the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railway for the past few years, and compare them with the information given before the special rate committee last year by President Beatty and President Hanna, he will be quite convinced that grain was handled at a very large profit by the railways, even under the prevailing rates. If it can be handled at a profit on the prairies, there is no reason in the world

Supply-Railways-C.N.R.
why the Transcontinental cannot be used from Winnipeg east to take the overflow of grain.
I am not suggesting any discrimination against the port of Montreal, where they have the finest facilities probably of any port in the world, but with the amount of money the government has spent on the port at Quebec, with the excellent railway we have there-and the Transcontinental is a road which has been excellently built-and with the equipment they have, there is no reason in the world, to my mind, why a large part of the overflow grain cannot be carried by way of that port.
I think in all sections of the House there is a great deal of sympathy for the western farmer, particularly in the marketing of cattle. We have just recently secured an opening for our cattle in the British market, which means a great deal to us. It will mean all the difference between profit and loss in raising these cattle, if we can ship them from the port of Quebec. It is very, very important, but if we have to pay a bonus of $600 to a steamship company to stop there for every shipment, it is no use to us. It would amount to $1.25 a head if we had to pay that sum, and that much extra deducted from the small profit, or added to the loss, means a great deal to the western farmer. I think the government can do us a very great service in this matter by approaching the managing officials of the Canadian National Railways and trying to see if it is not possible to get the usual rate-I do not suggest any lower rate-prevailing on the prairies, for the transportation of grain from Winnipeg to the port of Quebec. If there is a sufficient amount of grain to be handled vessels can call at that port, and in this way we can get our cattle shipped without any extra bonus. In addition to the saving of the bonus there will be a saving in the freight paid on cattle from Montreal to Quebec, because in the shipment I mentioned they had to pay, in addition to the bonus, the,full freight from Montreal to Liverpool. I trust the government will try to do something in this connection.	,

I moved this afternoon that this item should stand, pending the presentation to the committee of certain information which many of us believe the committee has the right to demand. That motion was ruled out of order. I then appealed to the minister to allow the item to stand until he was in possession of this information and submitted it to the House. This he refused to do. The minister then endeavoured to divert the attention of the committee from the immediate subject under discussion, and to introduce the question of an attack on the Canadian National Railways as a whole. In order to avoid that, and to make it clear that we do not attack the Canadian National Railways as a whole, I purpose moving, seconded by Mr. Boys, in protest against the manner in which the minister has endeavoured to put this item through, that item 139 be reduced by the sum of $2,000,000. That is the only way in which we feel we can formally and properly bring our protest before the committee, inasmuch as the other motion which reflected our views more accurately was ruled out of order.

I wish to reply to my hon. friend from Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell). No man in this House is any more delighted to hear what he said about the port of Quebec than myself. The development of that port when I happened to be Minister of Railways before was a hobby of mine. It was a little mutilated by the successors of the then government, and the plan as outlined by the government of which I had the honour of being a member, headed by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who represented Quebec, was changed, I think not for the benefit of the port of Quebec. But it has been .changed and certain advantages given to other railways that were not at all intended. However, the Transcontinental, I think I am safe in saying, is in good physical condition-at least I am so informed-and anything that can be done to increase the traffic over the Transcontinental to the port of Quebec will receive my hearty support. The fact that cattle can be landed there quickly by the Transcontinental and shipped has been proven, I think, very recently. As a matter of fact, I do not pose as a farmer.
The only man in the House that does not.
Now do not misunderstand me. Of course, I mean that everybody else does. Why not I?
I said that the minister was the only man in the House that did not pose as a farmer.

Then I will not say what I was going to say, but I think I am safe in saying that speed on the rails is a factor in the proper delivery of live stock, because the longer they are on the hoof in the car the greater their deterioration-I mean in regard to shrinkage in weight and so on. Anything I can do to improve conditions along that line I can assure my hon. friend I will be delighted to undertake, because I believe in the port of Quebec, and I believe in the

Transcontinental as the line to reach that port. My hon. friend (Mr. Stevens) has moved that this vote be reduced by $2,000,000. I want to tell hon. gentlemen that they are not interfering with the $2,000,000 but that they are crippling the management of the Canadian National Railways to the extent of $2,000,000. Some of the things that they probably want to do, it will be impossible to do, but that is beside the question. The situation is just as it was before. I cannot say anything more than I have said. My right hon. friend would do exactly the same thing if he were in my place; he could not do anything else.
I would do a great deal more.

Along the same line,
I think he would do a great deal less, because that is his history-give no information.
Rule 17B.

I can go back two or
three years in Hansard, and that is the principle laid down by my right hon. friend.

As regards day-to-day
operation, my hon. friend can read Hansard for five years back and he will find nothing different.

That would be a waste
of time.
It would be if he were trying to find anything different.

I say that the principle
that would be adopted by any great company in regard to the president of it, the position that Sir Henry Thornton is in, and the principle my right hon. friend would have to take were he in my place, would be that this being an uncompleted transaction and the president and the solicitor assuring me that, in their belief, to give these details at the present moment until the transaction was completed, would be detrimental to the Canadian National Railways, no other stand is possible than to abide by that advice. Who is to give me advice in regard to the Canadian National? My right hon. friend? No. I would not think it was good. The man whom the country has engaged to run the Canadian National Railways? If his advice is not good legally, then he has an adviser in the person of Mr. Ruel, I think one of the best-I will leave it at that-railway lawyers, at least, and business lawyers in the Dominion of Canada. His advice is the same as that of Sir. Henry Thornton: Knowing the inside of the transaction, he considers that

it would be injurious to the Canadian National Railways if the details which are asked for were made public. They are not merely for this House; they are intended for publication the world over as they would be published, and the opinion of these gentlemen is that that would be injurious to the Canadian National Railways. These men have advised me so. If you were in my place, what would you do? The responsibility is on the man whom we have hired to accept the responsibility, and I am not going to allow it to be put on my shoulders. I am taking the advice of these gentlemen. To reduce the estimate by $2,000,000 will not affect the transaction in any degree; it will only reduce the amount of money we can expend on betterments, buying of stock or anything of that kind for the Canadian National system. We have discussed this matter thoroughly; the committee has expressed its views; there is no portion of this committee that has not had full opportunity to place its protest on record; but as a principle of business that will be followed by any company, I say that the details should not be given out at the present moment, and I say that on the advice of the president of the company and his solicitor.
Did the minister, as head of the department of government purchasing this property, ask for a valuation of it?

I did not purchase the
property.

The government advanced $2,000,000 in connection with or in relation to the purchase. That is broad enough. The security that the country has, if there be any failure to complete this transaction, is this property. We have heard that over and over again. Has the government had any valuation made of this property?
The government did not buy the property.
I quite understand that.
The Canadian National Railway Company through their agent bought it-I should not say that.
It very nearly slipped out.

My hon. friend has said it so often; when you hear a story often you sometimes believe it. The Canadian National advanced the money for an agent to buy the property. Their judgment, the judgment of the president-and he has been in the pro-

perty very recently and knows the location -although my hon. friend says it is not on the main street-is that there are so many main streets in Paris that one cannot select one. Without fear of successful contradiction, I say that it is possibly in the best situation in Paris. I must assume that the president of the Canadian National Railways before he advanced the money, knew what he was doing, and I intend to leave the responsibility on his shoulders.
Had the Canadian National Railways any independent appraisal of the property made?

He can put it in writing if that is his opinion.
Surely my right hon. friend will accept a statement made on my responsibility.

Mr. Ruel did not understand what the minister said if he made any

I have that opinion, not in writing; but my right hon. friend surely sees his peculiar position. He says that this was bought without an order in council.
Without authority.
Put it in any way you like. but in the face of that, I assure the committee that Mr. Ruel, as legal adviser of the Canadian National Railways, assured me that this was perfectly legal.
Let me put it in this way, if I canot get the minister to get the opinion: Does the minister think it ought to be legal-
Oh, oh.

Hon. gentlemen have a strange idea of a joke and just as strange an idea of the law. Does the minister think it ought to be legal that the management or the directorate of the Canadian National Railways should be allowed to buy a $2,000,000 property in Paris without the knowledge of the government and prior vote of parliament?
All I am saying is what it is, and I did not frame the law.
I am asking the question: Does the minister think it ought to be?

My own view quite frankly would be that it would be better for such transactions as that to be made after consultation with the government, even to the extent of an order in council. I have no hesitation in saying that.
If the minister thinks it should not be the law, supposing it is, is he prepared to bring down legislation to amend the present act so as to ensure that it does not remain the law?

I certainly will make inquiries as to the law; but my right hon. friend has so befuddled me during the last two days with insisting that 'the law has been broken, that this would require some consideration. If, however, I am advised by the Minister of Justice that it is legal for the board or the president or any of the officials to purchase property without the consent of the government, I would suggest that the act should be amended so that this would not be legal.
I would like to see anything devised that is plainer than the present act.

know the facts of the case,, he does not know whether the Canadian National Railway has bought this property or has an option on it.

But he says he is advised by counsel for the railway that the transaction is perfectly legal.
