If there is one man in this House, Mr. Chairman, who ought to know everything about the Canadian National Railway legislation it is the right hon. leader of the Opposition. He framed that law, he brought it before the House, and if I remember rightly he defended it.
The National Railway Act?
No, the hon. gentleman's memory is rather wrong there. I did not introduce the bill, I did not frame it, and I had no particular connection with it except as a member of the government.
If I remember correctly, the right hon. gentleman took part in the debate on the bill and defended it.

I think so. I am proud
of that.

Anyway, the right hon.
gentleman was a member of the government at that time, therefore he knew of the bill before it was introduced, and according to the rules of our constitution he was responsible for the legislation in common with his colleagues. The main argument put forward by the right hon. leader and his friends is that this is an illegal transaction. I have the act before me. I do not claim to be a great lawyer, but I should like the right hon. leader of the Opposition to point out once for all anything in this law upon which he can base his assertion that the transaction in question is illegal. I do not see anything in the law to warrant his statement. The hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) last night argued that the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways had exactly the same powers and privileges as the directorate of an ordinary company. Is there anything in the Railway Act which says that the board of directors of a railway company cannot purchase a property without being authorized beforehand by their shareholders? I do not think that any such provision is to be found there. I say, therefore, that according to the Canadian National Railway law, introduced by the friends of the right hon. leader of the Opposition, there is absolutely nothing to prevent the Canadian National Railway board from doing what it has done.
I do not wish to repeat the argument which I made yesterday, but I think it would be a good thing for the members of this committee to bear in mind that the government to-day is simply putting into application the law which was framed, the law which was defended and the law which was first put into force by my right hon. friend and his associates. Why should the opposition today come before this committee and denounce this transaction as scandalous, when it has been put through in accordance with the law passed by the government of which the right hon. gentleman was a shining member? A minute ago the leader of the Opposition was asking my hon. friend, the Minister

Supply-Railways-C.N.R.
*of Railways (Mr. Graham) to amend .the law. Why was the law framed as it stands to-day if it is so bad? Why did my right hon. friend give to Mr. Hanna and the former directors of the Canadian National Railway board the powers which are contained in the law of 1919, and seek to deny those powers to Sir Henry Thornton and his board of directors to-day?
I shall not go into the merits of this transaction, I do not claim that it is good or bad, but I say that the government cannot be held responsible for such a transaction, and I can only conclude that the opposition in the attitude it has taken is simply playing a political game. I am a politician myself, I do not claim to be a statesman, but when I play politics I play it openly and I say so. Why should our friends on the other side claim that they wish to save the country from a tremendous catastrophe when they are simply playing the ordinary game of politics?
I have in my hand, Mr. Chairman, the Journals of the House of Commons of 1921. On the 22nd of March, 1921, the Liberal opposition, of which I was a member, was desirous of securing certain information with respect to how the Canadian National railways were being run. We thought that parliament should be furnished with certain particulars and certain details as to the management. My right hon. friend was a minister at that time, and the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) was also a minister. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) was a member of the House, as was the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion). All these gentlemen whom we have heard since last night asking for information, asking for particulars, saying that this vote should not go through unless all the documents connected with the transaction were laid on the Table-what did all these gentlemen say when we asked for information? At that time Sir George Foster moved that we go into Committee of Supply, and the then leader of the Opposition, now Prime Minister, moved:
Subject to the reservation that in exceptional cases there may be documents of a confidential character which, in the public interest, may properly be withheld from publication, the House deolares that it is the undoubted right of parliament to demand and receive copies of all reports, accounts, correspondence and papers in relation to the management of every department of the public service including the affairs of the Canadian National Railways, whether operating directly under the control of the department, *or under corporate form.
We voted-
Did you vote for that?

Certainly I voted for it, and I have not since changed my opinion. My opinion is very simply stated: I say that this parliament should be given every information that is not of a confidential character or the disclosing of which would not be detrimental to the public interest. The stand I took then is the stand I take to-day, and that is what the resolution meant. We were simply asking that any information that was not confidential or the furnishing of which would not be detrimental to the public interest should be made available to parliament, and these gentlemen not only denied us the right to have information that was not of a confidential character, but said that we were entitled to no information whatsoever.
Oh, no.

The resolution is right here; my right hon. friend can read it. Now, Mr. Chairm^, to show how sincere these gentlemen are to-day in their attitude in this fight they are putting up, I would ask you to read the list of those who voted on the division which followed the presentation [DOT] of the resolution to which I have referred. Where was the right hon. leader of the Opposition on this question? Was he then, as he is to-day, in favour of information being given to representatives of the people? Where was the member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton)? Where was my eloquent friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) and my also eloquent friend from Fort William (Mr. Manion)? They were on the side of those who denied the representatives of the people the least information.
Now, if this is going to be a fight as a party question, let us fight it out. We are not afraid; this is not our first battle. But the right hon. leader of the Opposition reminds me of a god whose name I have forgotten but of whom I read in my Greek mythology. It was a god who used to eat his own children so as to preserve their father. Who, Mr. Chairman, is the father of this Canadian National system? The right hon. gentleman. In 1912 in this House, in the words of the then member for Calgary, he was the "gramaphone of Mackenzie and Mann;" he carried through the legislation which was afterwards denounced all over Canada. He is' the gentleman who, in the House of Commons, burdened the people of Canada with every debt, every obligation incurred by the Canadian Northern and by Mackenzie and Mann. Who is the man who forced on the people of Canada the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk system? The right hon. gentleman. Who brought these

Supply-Railways-C.N.R.

children into the world? He was their father; but to-day, in order to preserve himself politically, he wishes to swallow them. The Tory party is evidently playing the old game of leaning on the Canadian Pacific Railway so as to kill the Canadian National Railway and preserve its own existence. If the right hon. gentleman wishes to be in this House, having been the father of the Canadian National Railway, the representative of the Canadian Pacific Railway, it is his own business. But I do not think the people of Canada are ready to follow the right'hon. gentleman in his political game.
One last word: Not only did these gentlemen refuse us any information when they were in power-information of any nature,-but to-day they say a great principle is at stake, the principle whether public moneys are to be expended by the directorate of the Canadian National Railway without previous consultation with the government or with parliament. Well, if that principle is so sacred, i# it is of such importance, how is it that when these gentlemen were in power they expended $72,000,000 in building up a merchant marine without even calling for tenders? Was parliament consulted when the Hon. Mr. Ballantyne, then Minister of Marine, expended $72,000,000 to build up a merchant marine? Coming to the question of liability the hon. member says, and wisely he predicated it upon the modest assumption that he was Dot a good lawyer, unless you could show him something in the act that denies Sir Henry Thornton the right to buy a hotel in Paris, he had it, and he ought to exercise it. liament. I opposed it, and rightly opposed it, and I would oppose it now. Hon. members opposite, I suppose, had they been in office then might have supported it and then when the time came when information was wanted they would do as they are doing now, tell us it is "confidential". speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
I must say
that I have heard my right hon. friend on many occasions speaking in the positive way in which he always addresses the House and making assertions with that bold manner which he always summons to his aid no matter whether the subject may be a serious one or comparatively unimportant. But we have heard it explicitly declared, respecting this act in connection with the Canadian National Railways that expenditures such as were proposed by Sir Henry Thornton to be made in Paris could not be made, because of their character without the direct sanction of the government. My hon. friend from Dorchester very properly said to-night to my right hon. friend that he could not find any such declaration within the four comers of that statute. The right hon. gentleman then proceeded to declare that that declaration was made and was to be found in section 23 of the act. When I ventured to interrupt my right hon. friend and to state that that declaration could not be found in section 23 of the act, he intimated that my interruptions were of no value whatever. Then I asked him if there were any other sections in which he could find legal justification for this position that he and his desk mates have been taking for the last two days, and then he admitted it was not in the act at all. And when he declared that it was not in the act at all. It is not in the act. My right hon. friend cannot find within the four corners of this act any statement, or any provision in the statute, which made it obligatory upon Sir Henry Thornton, as the president of this railway, to come to the governor in council for absolute authority before he proceeded to negotiate for the purchase of this property in Paris. So that we have that much in the way of clearing the air of all this mist, innuendo and suspicion which is being engendered by hon. members on the other side of the House for the last two days. What next? We had repeated demands that my hon. friend the Minister of Railways would explain clearly to the committee the attitude of the government in reference to the management of the Canadian National; but we have committed the task to Sir Henry Thornton, we are holding him responsible for the results and we are not interfering with him in regard to the plans he may make or the ideas he may conceive, in order that the end and aim of the Canadian people as a whole might be attained in regard to the successful operation of the railway.
My hon. friend does not think to-day as he thought a few years ago. There is nothing that my hon. friend resents so much as a charge of inconsistency and yet upon this very question, when we come to consider the point as to what information the Minister of Railways should give this House and the country with reference to the operation of the .Canadian National by Sir Henry Thornton, we find that my hon. friend laid down two years ago a totally different doctrine from that which he lays down to-day and I will prove that statement. My right hon. friend speaking on a motion proposed at that time by my right hon. leader went on to speak as to the nature of the information that

-they will be put under a disability that their great competitor is not under at all. general manager who would be big enough for the tremendous task of operating that system to-day would undertake to assume such responsibility under conditions that would be brought about were this amendment adopted.

speechtext:
My hon. friend may not be in such a hilarious mood when I get through. He says:
I know there must be 6uch information at that time as will enable parliament properly to judge as to the general management of the system and to say whether or not the Board of Directors that we have put in charge have in the main properly discharged the responsibility placed upon them. That information must be given; but if this resolution passes, it is certain that much that is unfortunate will happen, but very improbable that what is most desirable will actually result. This resolution means simply a return to the old system of political control; it stops nowhere short of that end.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
What is the situation here? This government committed the control and the operation of the Canadian National Railways to Sir Henry Thornton and his board of directors. Now, I think Sir Henry Thornton enjoys the confidence of the people of this country since he has assumed the management of that road. I think the care with which he has approached the solution of all the internal problems which face this country in regard to this railway, and the evident interest which he has taken in regard to all these matters indicates that we are justified, as members of this government, in believing that Sir Henry Thornton, to-day has the confidence of the Canadian people. Sir Henry Thornton, coming from the other side, knows that Canada cannot be a hermit nation, and that the great success of the Canadian Pacific Railway has been due to the fact that, on account of their ocean steamships, they are the great highway of the world between the eastern and western hemispheres, and that the ramifications of that system on the Continent, as any hon. member who has ever been over there will realize, furnish the very life blood of the Canadian Pacific Railway. If under Sir Henry Thornton's management we are to attain that success in government ownership which every man in this country, if he is a true patriot ought to hope for, is it not natural for Sir Henr>
Thornton to say "As a means to that end, on the continent of Europe, I must obtain some business connections which will enable me to be, at least, a competitor with the Canadian Pacific Railway on that continent?" I venture to say that the doctrines laid

Supply-Railways


down by the right hon. member which I quote to-night, expressed to this House so definitely two years ago on this very question as to what ought to be the policy in dealing with the matter of operation, are in direct conflict with his statements to-night, because he declared at that time that these matters should not be the subject of communication to parliament before they were consummated.
And what more? Let me submit, Mr. Chairman, the lines upon which the right hon. gentleman laid down the importance of maintaining the secrecy of business connections in the business management of a great enterprise. These are the lines which he laid down. My right hon. friend says to the Minister of ""Railways, by a succession of innuendoes, that Sir Henry Thornton had no business to consider the question of purchasing an hotel in Paris. It has been stated by the right hon. member and reiterated for two days that the law declared that that was so, and he had no such power, and now he cannot put his finger upon the law. Hon. gentlemen on the other side and, in particular, my right hon. friend have stressed the name of Mr. Aronovici, as if some virtue was to be obtained by reiterating the name of a man who had been the purchasing agent of one of the greatest English railways, as negotiating this matter on behalf of the president of the National Railways. My hon. friend says, as regards this general appropriation which the Minister of Railways is asking from ;parliament this year for the operation of railways in Canada: "Oh, we want to have that reduced until we get that information," information similar to that which two years ago he declared, if it were given, would have meant putting the railways under political control. Information of this character he now wants to have. I think the Minister of Railways was quite right when he pointed out to the committee shortly before dinner what was at the bottom of this whole question. Either my right hon. friend was right or half right in 1921 when he laid down the simple business rule that, in the management of a great enterprise, it was only right and proper that a certain amount of secrecy should attach to negotiations until they were concluded, or he is wrong now. Sir Henry Thornton enjoys the confidence of the Canadian people. He has started upon this proposition in connection with obtaining continental business. Either we are to trust his judgment in that regard or we are not. If it is not a good thing for him to look abroad across the channel and endeavour to find avenues by which men and women of the
Continent who want to travel across the ocean' to Canada, or beyond Canada to cross the Pacific also, can do so; if it is not sound business for him to do that, then the position is a very singular one. This must be sound business, and if in the carrying out of that idea of sound business, he is to be asked, in the course of negotiations, to satisfy the curiosity of my right hon. friend and his desk-mate as regards everyone to whom he has talked, everything he has talked about and all these things that have taken place during the consideration of the proposition, surely that is not wise. We on this side of the House trust and believe in Sir Henry Thornton. We think it is in the interest of the Canadian people that he should be given an opportunity to make good. He has been in Canada for a matter of only some four, five or six months, and already there is evidence of renewed impulse to the railways and renewed confidence amongst the Canadian people. As regards this matter we say to this committee that we think it should trust to Sir Henry Thornton's judgment. We believe results will justify his action, and we think the motion of the hon. gentleman in regard to the reduction of this item and the attitude of the right hon. gentleman are, as they were declared to be by the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon), purely a matter of playing politics.
Will the minister inform the committee whether, in his opinion, this is a capital expenditure or not?

speechtext:
I say this
to my hon. friend that there has been no expenditure in regard to this matter.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I say further that my hon. friend probably did not catch my point. Notwithstanding the hilariousness of those leaders of his, I challenge them to show where in the act there is any authority for what they have been stating. They are absolutely unable to do so.

It is with some hesitation that I enter intd a discussion of this subject. As to whether the expenditure in question was a wise one or not, I shall not with the present information I have at hand, presume to pronounce an opinion. Certainly I should not presume to pronounce an opinion 10 p.m. upon the legal aspect of the question; neither will I, in the course of my few remarks, impute to any person motives such as the playing of politics or any other motive than the welfare of the country. I have no desire to play politics regarding this
Supply-R ailways-C.N.R.

matter if I ever was inclined to such a course. I have, however, been intensely anxious to come to a proper conclusion regarding this question, andtf called upon to cast a vote, to east a vote that will be justified in my own mind, and that I can justify to my constituents and the people of Canada generally. It has been urged upon us that if we vote against this expenditure which has been made, we are casting a vote against the interest of the Canadian National Railways. Whether that statement be true or not, it would not be fair to say to any persons that they are deliberately doing so. I would like to take it for granted that all hon. members in this House are desirous of seeing the Canadian National Railways a success. Yet it is quite possible that injury may be done to that system even if we do not do so by deliberate intent.
This question has brought to us one of the most difficult problems connected with our National Railways; that is the question as to how far we can give to those to whom we have entrusted the management of our railways similar powers to those possessed by Mr. Beatty and his associates in the management of the great Canadian Pacific railway, and at the same time secure for the shareholders represented by their representatives here in parliament, those rights which naturally reside in the shareholders of a great company. I think I am right in saying that that is the most difficult problem which we have to face, to know just at what point to draw the line between giving a free hand to those managing our railway system, and at the same time reserving our rights as representatives of the owners of the system.
Perhaps even to define this by statute would be one of our most difficult problems, and I am quite willing to say this that, perhaps, the present statute, if it is interpreted by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen), that there is a distinction between capital expenditure and operating charges, gives the wisest distinction that can be made. Whether that distinction is made in the law as it stands, I am not, as I said before, going to pronounce an opinion. Granting, however, that that is a correct interpretation of $he law, I think I can imagine that an occasion might arise where even the letter of the law might need to be violated. I think I can imagine that a situation might arise that would necessitate a violation of the strict letter of the law. The extent to which we might condone such a violation would of course have to be determined by the circumstances of the case as they arose.
When the government made the announcement to the country that they were going to LMr. Brown.]
give Sir Henry Thornton a free hand in the management of the railways, I think the whole country from the Atlantic to the Pacific gave their approval to such a declaration. To me there is in the whole situation in Canada to-day nothing that I look upon as more necessary to our ultimate well-being than that our government railways should be made a success. We desire the success of the Canadian National Railways; but success will depend on many different factors; it will depend on the loyalty with which the people of Canada support those roads, and I believe there is in the country an increasing feeling of loyalty towards that institution.
I believe it is quite correct to say that if we go among the people we shall find a growing sentiment that they feel "This is something that belongs to us." And I think there is a growing feeling of optimism, a feeling that success can ultimately be achieved. But while a number of factors enter into the success of the road, it seems to me the outstanding factor will be the capacity and the capability of the man we put at the head of the system. In other words, we have to rely upon Sir Henry Thornton. Now, the question that must necessarily come up in our minds is, to what extent are we willing to trust the man that we have placed at the head of the system. As I look upon the situation to-day I think I am willing to take this position, that if Sir Henry Thornton does not make a success of this system, then it is inevitably doomed to failure. I believe we are now just at that critical stage, that it is a case of succeed or fail, and if Sir Henry Thornton does not make a success of our Canadian National Railways I doubt the possibility of getting any other man to do so. That is, if I correctly estimate Sir Henry Thornton, he is a man that would not very long put up with too much nagging. And the man who would put up with much nagging would not likely be the type of man that would make a success of this system.
I believe there is danger in a man becoming unduly autocratic, there is dagger in his going too far in the reckless expenditure of the people's money. I realize that danger, and I do not need any person in this House or outside to impress upon me the danger that confronts us in that direction. But to my mind the greatest danger that faces our National Railway system to-day is undue political interference. That, to my mind is infinitely a more imminent danger than any other that can possibly arise. With that thought in my mind, and holding the views I have expressed, I am disposed, with our present limited knowledge of this transaction,

Supply-Railways-C.NJl.
to give Sir Henry Thornton a fairly free hand. The time will come when fuller information will no doubt be disclosed to us. At the moment I am not disposed to condone this particular transaction, I think it is quite evident that in some aspects it merits our disapprobation, but at the same time, holding as I do that the greatest danger confronting our National Railways is undue political interference, I feel disposed to give Sir Henry Thornton the benefit of every reasonable doubt. I think if Sir Henry Thornton is the man that we take him to be he is capable of rising to his great opportunities. I do not know if he is likely to hear what I say or take any notice of it if he does, but I think he has the greatest opportunity that any man ever had in the commercial or industrial world. He has to take hold of this National Railway system, handicapped it is true by tremendous over-capitalization, and to make it a success. We pay him a salary, and properly so, that gives him the pos-sibilitj^ of enjoying everything in life that any man needs to enjoy, and we offer him, as I say, an opportunity of doing the biggest thing that any man has ever dona in the commercial or industrial world-an opportunity of doing something, not for himself but for the good of the Canadian people. If Sir Henry Thornton rises to the opportunity that is given to him, as I believe he is a big enough man to do, he can estab'ish for himself a name before which the names of Ford, Rockefeller and other men who have accumulated great fortunes for themselves will look small indeed.
Can the hon. member tell me how much Sir Henry Thornton has at stake in the Canadian National Rail-vray system compared with the people of Canada?

His reputation. The opportunity has been given to him not only to sustain his reputation but to make a still greater reputation for himself, a reputation that will be the greatest that any man has ever achieved in the commercial and industrial world. That is what I think he has at stake. While it may be possible-I do not know at present-that he has been led into a transaction which is in violation of the strict letter of the law, for myself I propose to withhold judgment on the merits of this particular case until full information is given to us.
In regard to the amendment itself, the minister has stated that its acceptance would not affect the transaction in any way at all, but would simply mean curtailing th6 expenditure of the board for the coming year and crippling their work to the extent of $2,000,000. If that be the correct statement of the case, holding as we from the West do, the necessity for the immediate construction of many branch lines-there are many sections out there in need of railway facilities-for my part, even if I were disposed to support the amendment on other grounds, I could not consent to do so now and in any way cripple the management of the Canadian National Railways for the coming year.

speechtext: That is not the act.

It is the estimate I am reading from, which becomes an act when it is passed by parliament. I read a moment ago from the statute, not from the estimates of last year; the latter are in the Appropriation Act. It is chapter 53 of the acts of last session to which I referred.

speechtext: It is not in the Canadian National Railway Act.

No, in the Appropriation Act, in which the limitation is expressly defined. Now, I take the vote of this year and I find not identically the same language, but language that is similar and of the same . effect. I read from item 139, at the top of page 32 of the Estimates. The language is:
The amount herein authorized may be applied from time to time, in the discretion of the Governor in Council.
And what was that amount for? How may that money be used? Turn to page 31: "(a) Operating deficits; (b) acquisition of property." That would cover the present case; it is the same express limitation of last year. Now, such a limitation upon the expenditure of that money, can it be argued for a moment that Sir Henry Thornton can take that amount out of the treasury without the authority of an order in council or the consent of the minister? It passes my comprehension how that can be done. Let me just touch upon the other question. The powers of the Canadian National Railway Board as it exists are set forth in the Act of 1919. Only such powers as are set forth in that act can be exercised by that company; it gets them all there; it has no existence whatever apart from that statute. What did we give
[Mr. Guthrie. 1
to the company? I shall not read the sections, but we gave them the management and the operation of the lines of railway; that is the meaning of section 11. Then follow the restrictions: They cannot acquire new lines of railway without going to the Governor in Council for authority. They cannot amalgamate with other companies, they cannot issue securities, without going to the Governor in Council for authority. All they can do is to look after the management and operation of the road. I quite agree with the Minister of Railways in his interpretation of the. act; I heard him on two occasions plainly give it as his opinion this was a capital expenditure and that capital expenditure could not regularly be made without the matter having first come before the minister and the Governor in Council. Well, apart from the National Railway Act, what about the vote of this parliament? Are the express terms and conditions under which parliament voted that money to be absolutely disregarded by the head of this railway board? Is he to be supreme? Is he to be above parliament or the votes of parliament? Is the limitation which we impose by act of parliament when we vote the money to be of no effect? I do not know whether the purchase was wise or was unwise; it is beyond me. I know I heard with a great deal of satisfaction the minister say to-day that the thing would not occur again. It is easy to see from the attitude of the minister that had he been consulted in the matter the transaction would never have gone through in the manner in which it did. But what I maintain is that there has been a breach of the letter and of the spirit of the National Railway Act; there has been a breach of the limitations imposed by this parliament when we voted the money. It was a wrong thing for Sir Henry Thornton to do. If in the opinion of the committee he should be excused, that is another question, but I do not think the offence should be condoned. I believe some reprimand should be offered under all these circumstances. For my part I am willing to leave the reprimand entirely in the hands of the Minister of Railways. I think he both feels and sees the real situation and realizes that there is something very wrong in the whole transaction.

Mr. Chairman, I do not know that anybody could contribute much that is new or informative to this debate. The remarks of the Prime Minister this afternoon and those of the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) just a little while ago represent my views upon this matter, and I

Supply-Railways-C.N.R.
think each of them has plotted out the course that parliament should follow in this particular case. The leader of the Opposition (Mr Meighen) and the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Guthrie) asserted on several occasions this evening that there was no legal warrant for the purchase made by Sir Henry Thornton, president of the National Railways. Even if there were not legal authority for the course pursued, I doubt if the country generally would be much exercised over that fact; if the expenditure itself was sound, parliament and the country would condone the transaction But I wish to say with the same amount of confidence that was shown by the leader of the Opposition and by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) that the action taken is well within the statute. Whether it is wise to incur expenditures of this magnitude without direct contact with the government may be, of course, a question for debate. Now, section 23 has been referred to several times. Clearly that clause is not relevant to the issue; it merely gives the company power to construct and operate railways- under the authority of the Governor in Council. That is not the case we are discussing. There is another section, 29, which authorizes the company to purchase the securities or shares of going businesses which are incidental to the work of a railway, such as hotel businesses or electric power businesses. That is not this case, and that section is not applicable. Section 11 is perhaps the most important section, and it has been referred to by the hon. member for South Wellington. May I read that again:
The Governor in Council may from time to time by order in council entrust to the company the management and operation of any lines of railway or parts thereof.
That section entrusts to the company the power of operating and managing the Canadian National Railways. That company therefore has the same powers that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company has in the operation of its property. It has all the powers that any other railway company in Canada has, and I ask hon. gentlemen if it is not well within the legal and statutory powers of boards of directors of railway companies to rent offices, to build offices for the company's purposes. The directors of this company have exactly the same powers that the directors of any other railway company in Canada has, and I submit with confidence there can be no question as to the powers of the directors of a company to purchase buildings for the company's own purposes. I do not think that is open to question.
Then there is another section, section 16 which provides:
Notwithstanding anything in the Government Railways Act or the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, all expenses incurred in connection with the operation or management of the Canadian Government Railways, under the provisions of this act, shall be paid out of the receipts and revenues of the Canadian Government Railways.
Now the question is if the acquisition of a building in Paris for the purposes of the company's offices is necessary to the prudent and aggressive management of the company. Surely such expenditure would come within that section, and a deficit would require to be liquidated by a vote of this parliament. The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat has referred to the estimates to be voted in connection with the Canadian National Railways this session. I submit that whether this transaction is lawful or not is to be determined by the statute of 1919 in reference to the Canadian National Railways, and not by the verbiage accompanying a proposed vote in parliament. It is true that when it comes into the Appropriation Act it has the effect of a statute, but even in that instance it provides for the payment of the deficit, and if the purchase of this property is responsible for incurring a portion of that deficit then I think the vote which the hon. member read supports the contention which I have made.
Now just a few words as to the transaction itself. The purchase of this building may indicate a great deal of courage, excellent judgment and prevision on the part of Sir Henry Thornton. It may be a bold and splendid conception and one that will ultimately prove of value to the country and to our railway system. The transaction may conform with the usual and best business practices known to us to-day, and yet it is one that is liable to misinterpretation and misrepresentation, and that, Mr. Chairman, is one of the difficulties of government ownership and government operation. It will always be difficult for the Canadian National Railways to do the right thing in connection with the big things in a proper way because a critical public and a critical parliament will not accord to them the same freedom of action and of judgment that is usually accorded to business men and to the directors and managers of a big concern.
Now what are the facts? So far as I can gather them by a reading of Hansard chiefly, I would suppose the facts to be somewhat as follows: Sir Henry Thornton, the president of the Canadian National Railways, believed it was in the interests of the company

Supply-Railways-C.N.R.

to have an office well located in the city of Paris, to be the centre possibly of their European operations. I gather also that it was their intention to lease from somebody else this particular building, and that at a certain stage negotiations were on for the purchase of this property by a syndicate. It transpired that another purchaser was in the field whom they feared might purchase the property and prevent the Canadian National Railways from obtaining it for rental purposes. In consequence of that Sir Henry Thornton had to act quickly, and from the current funds of the Canadian National Railways he advanced $2,000,000 to purchase this property, not to hold the property, but to give him temporary ownership while he undertook the organization of a syndicate outside to take over the property and lease to the company such portion of it as they desired for the purposes of the company. I see my friend angularly opposite to me smiling.
It is a great joke.
But these things are done every day by reputable business men, by the ablest business men in the world.
With public money?

I will come to that in a minute. They do it every day, and if it is sound in their case why is it unsound in this particular instance? Let me proceed a little further. I stated that when Sir Henry Thornton secured possession of the property he contemplated the organization of a purchasing syndicate to take it over and to lease from them a portion of the building for the purposes of the company. That is done every day, and I say that there is nothing objectionable in it, and if he did not do it, who else would do it? I admit that the whole circumstances permit the suspicious mind to create a false picture of this whole transaction. Hon. gentlemen want some more information. What further information do they want? What further information would be of any good to them?
We have not any yet.

Am I not right in saying that they are praying they will not receive any because it might spoil the whole purpose of their argument of yesterday and to-day? If the facts disclosed that this proposed purchasing syndicate belonged to the city of New York they would say, why not have organized a Canadian syndicate? The 
fact probably is that you could not organize a syndicate in Canada at the present time to engage in such a transaction. You probably would require to go to a large city where very large sums of money for investment purposes were available. If the syndicate was a Canadian syndicate, what would happen? Somebody in it would be found to be the thirty-second cousin of someone connected with the railway or the forty-second cousin of some member on this side of the House or of a member of the government. Already the leader of the Opposition is playing upon the name of the man in whose name the property is now held, and I fancy one could make an interesting and destructive political speech on that fact alone. If the leader of the New York syndicate had the Hebraic name of Moses as my right hon. friend has suggested, that might afford ample ground for political pamphlets and many political speeches.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that if Sir Henry Thornton believed it was in the interests of the company to own a property in Paris he pursued the only course open to him. I am not sure whether it is advisable to have an office in Paris at the present time. Perhaps it is. I am not to be judge of that. Sir Henry Thornton is the adviser of this country in this particular matter, and I submit that we must accept his judgment. And probably the idea is a sound one. It may be a very big idea and worthy of being carried out. If the Canadian National Railways have an active organization in Paris it may be worth 100 or 500 commercial agents in Europe. It may not only be the representative there of the railway system itself, but it will be the agent of the men of business in this country, and will be an active propagandist for the development of our trade in European countries. I would urge upon hon. gentlemen not to disparage, and damage and destroy a transaction that seems a perfectly natural one and one that is engaged in almost every day by large railway or industrial companies. I assume-I am bound to assume, and I think every hon. member in the House should assume-that Sir Henry Thornton has acted in good faith in this matter and really has at heart the interest of the National Railways and nothing else. He does not anticipate a permanent capital investment; evidently he will shortly be recouped the temporary advance which he secured through the bank on behalf of the railways, and the railway treasury will then be repaid the advance. I assume again that Sir Henry Thornton will be in a position bn that it is carried through.

Now it may be, Mr. Chairman, as I said before, and as I think the Minister of Railways said, that in transactions of this size it would be better that before the transaction is launched or completed, full negotiation and discussion should take place with the government, or at least with the Minister of Railways. I feel, however, that Sir Henry Thornton deemed it to be an expenditure which should be made. In his judgment it is one that will enure to the advantage of the railways and to the country, and as it was only a temporary expenditure I think he should be supported. It would be very unfortunate if every transaction of the Canadian National Railways became the matter of a discussion in parliament. I do not deny the right of the opposition to engage in the criticism they have indulged in yesterday and to-day. They, perhaps, have only done their duty. They may have rendered a public service. They have, however, already said all they can say upon the question, and I do not think they are performing their duty in any better way than they have already done by moving an amendment and asking for a vote upon this particular item.

Having spoken before I almost regret to address the committee again upon this subject. I assure them that I would not do so if it were not for the very peculiar positions, taken by my hon. friend the Acting Minister of National Defence, and by my very good and hon. friend the member for Halifax who has just spoken. With reference to the latter, permit me to express the hope that when he shall be called to that eminent position to which the newspapers are at present appointing him, he will display perhaps not a more judicial attitude, but that at least the law administered by him will be of a much better brand than that which he has propounded to the committee tonight. I know that neither the Acting Minister of National Defence nor , the member for Halifax are at all oblivious of the decision of the court of Exchequer Chamber in the very well known law case of the Ashbury Company vs. Riche. What was that? An incorporation, under a British statute of a company to carry on railway operations, and when they undertook to buy a railway in Switzerland it was held beyond their powers. And yet had the court of Exchequer Chamber had the benefit of the eloquence of the Acting Minister of National Defence they would have been told in thunder tones that you could not find a line in the statute forbidding it. And no man of any standing as a practising barrister would expect to find a line in the statute forbidding
it. That is only what I must characterize as simply a bit of bluff put forward to help the government out of a difficult position. It is not law, it is bluff. That is what we got from the Acting Minister of National Defence to-night. Now, the case that I have spoken of stands. It is law. It is not a matter of politics, it is a rule to which all people in the British Empire must submit in the construction of a matter of this kind; and that rule applies just as much to the construction of the act relating to the Canadian National Railways as it does to anything else. In this case there is a company incorporated, and what is it incorporated for? I know that other hon. and learned gentlemen have addressed the committee on the subject, and at a good deal of length, and I do not propose to take up very much time, but I am going to point out something that I think has not been pointed out yet. We use a preamble in the statutes for the purpose of explaining, and circumscribing, and interpreting the rest of the statute, and in that very preamble-the preface, the reason that is given to this legislation-we are told that :
-it is expedient to provide for the incorporation of a company under which-
What now?
-the railways, works and undertakings of the companies comprised in the Canadian Northern system may be consolidated-
Now, that is present or past. It is something that has existed and still existsand together with the Canadian Government Railways operated as a National Railway system.
Does that indicate anything other than Canada? Does that suggest the carrying on of a railway in France? Could you have built a railway from Calais to Paris under that legislation? Did anybody ever think' of such a thing? The court of Exchequer Chamber burst that soap bubble fifty years ago. It has been blown again to-night to serve a very obvious purpose. Now then we have a company formed, and I am not going into the details of that except to say that it is not a one man company such as we sometimes hear spoken of. It is a railway board of directors, or is supposed to be so, and the gentle' man who is chairman is only one member of it; but the astonishing thing-leaving all other legal considerations out of the question- is that the Minister of Railways has not been able to point out to this House that the purchase, or transaction, or agreement, or whatever I may call this nebulous thing that has taken place, whatever it is, is not the act of the board of directors itself, not the act of the company; it is the act of one individual

unsupported by a resolution, unsupported by even the shadow of the company, and not reported to the minister. That is clear beyond the necessity of any further demonstration. It cannot be denied that if the minister could have had a resolution of the board of directors and brought it here he would have had some footing. But he has got nothing but the solitary personal act-however good the intention may have been, and I am not going to discuss that-nothing but the solitary personal act of Sir Henry Thornton uncommunicated to the minister and, as far as the evidence before this committee is concerned, uncommunicated to any one of his colleagues. That is what this House is asked to ratify and endorse as the usual, the ordinary and proper mode of conducting the business of the National Railways.
Is the committee prepared to accept that? Is the government prepared to stand back of it? I sympathize with and admire that attitude of the Minister of Railways, who clothing his statement in such language as is necessary to soften the blow, has practically told Sir Henry Thornton that this thing is not to occur again, and has assured the House that it will not occur again with his sanction. What am I to say of the group of apologists on the other side of the House, who have quoted everything from discussions in connection with matters pertaining to the National Railway, have quoted from my right hon. friend's remarks, and have almost given to a speech of his in the House a few years ago the solemnity of an act of parliament, and that from the same gentleman who denied that the act of 1921, because it dealt with finance, was an act of parliament, and treated it as only a resolution-a strange case of* mental confusion or moral obliquity, I do not know which. When we turn to section 11, to which the hon. senior member for Halifax has referred, we find the following:
The Governor in Council may from time to time by order in council entrust to the company the management and operation of any lines of railway or parts thereof, and any property or works of whatsoever description.
And so forth. We find nothing there about new construction. Hon. members will find a section that has not been referred to, that * permits the powers of expropriation to be exercised.
May I ask the bon. member a question?
Certainly.

If the cost of this building in Paris were $10,000 and not $2,000,000, would my hon. friend think that

the Canadian National Railway would not have legal authority to buy that for its own purposes?
What purposes?
The company's purposes.	.

Well I hope, when justice is administered in the Exchequer Court, that it will not be regulated by the number of dollars involved in the transaction, and that one matter will not be considered legal because only $10,000 is involved, and another matter considered illegal because $1,000,000 is involved. It would not be legal on account of the small amount involved. I cannot draw such a distinction.

The hon. member does not get my point. I wanted to test the soundness of his argument, and I think he might admit that it is not a sound argument. Does he seriously mean to say that the Canadian National Railway, without the authority of the Governor in Council, could not go to the city of Paris or to London and buy a building for $5,000 or $10,000 for its own purposes?

Leave the amount out of the question altogether. I thought the hon. member was drawing a distinction as to the amount. I say they have no legal authority to buy one square foot of land in Paris or anywhere else under this act.

Could they
lease an office, buy furniture and put it in?
No, they cannot carry on business.
I think my hon. friend, at the close of the sitting of the House this evening, should sit down and reason out the matter.

I will take the words of the Acting Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald), and I will employ them to better reasoning than he employed them. When considering the charter of the company, I will take what T find within the four comers of the act constituting the company, in order to find some provision authorizing a particular thing to be done. If it is not there, it follows that the thing is not authorized. I have not read every line of the act, but I have seen nothing that instances foreign countries as places where business may be carried on. I find in the act provision for expropriation, and I thought they might be referred to, because I find the plan may be signed by the minister or the

Supply-Railways-C.A'J?.
president or vice-president of the company. But if members were reading the act, and thought that it followed from the language that they could acquire property by expropriation-but of course that would be within Canada-without the consent of the Governor in Council, they would still be wrong, because the Railway Act permiting expropriation for railway purposes requires the preliminary consent of the minister before even the plan can be filed. If you read this act from end to end you will find it does not contain a single provision looking to the making of capital expenditure by this board, or the acquisition of property or anything of that kind, without the consent of the Governor in Council. Section 23 has been referred to and I need hardly repeat it, but it says:
With the approval of the Governor in Council and upon any location sanctioned by the Minister of Railways and Canals-
Will any hon. member say that that means in England, Scotland, Ireland or France?
-the company may from time to time construct and operate railway lines, branches and extensions or railway facilities or property of any description in respect to the construction whereof respectively, parliament may hereafter authorize the necessary expenditure or the guarantee of an issue of the company's securities.
When has parliament authorized the expenditure, assuming the company could lawfully expend money in France or in England? And when has the approval of the Governor General in Council been given?
As to the particular transaction, I do not know whether it is a building or not. The thing has become so absolutely nebulous that it may be a sort of dirigible balloon that is floating over Paris. I cannot get much accurate information. The need of this country is the handling of freight, passenger traffic is carried ordinarily at a loss by the railways, and the freight sustains the passenger traffic. All that I can see of this nebulous proposition is that somebody wants to advertise for passenger business. I cannot conceive what freight is going to be brought to the National Railways by this expenditure.	We cannot,
however, get any information. We are not even told the particular purpose. We are noc told how many rooms the railway is expected to occupy, or whether it is for freight or passenger business. That sort of thing cannot be a secret. If it were to be a secret it would have to be equally a secret that this is an hotel. Perhaps it is not. I sympathize with the position the minister is placed in when he can tell us so little about it, but I must make a protest against the misinterpretation of the statutes by the Acting Minister of National Defence and against the attempt
to influence members who do not profess to make law their vocation in life, to misrepresent the application of legal principles to the whole subject, particularly for the purpose of political excuse or political advantage.

In view of the fact that an amendment has been introduced, I wish to state my position with regard to that amendment. Last night I endeavoured to state my position on the general question. I have no desire whatever to cover .that ground again. As I listened a few minutes ago to the rather laboured defence put forward by the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) it seemed that there was full justification for a protest against the action that has been taken by Sir Henry Thornton. The senior member for Halifax suggested that the expenditure was but a temporary one, and on that ground no exception should be taken. It seems to me his argument might be used to carry him a great deal further than this particular case If, for example, in encouraging this tourist traffic from Paris, it might be considered advisable that some sort of a race track should be started or an amusement park or a seaside resort be opened, in that case it would seem to be quite justifiable that Sir Henry Thornton should take one or two million dollars to organize a syndicate to start some such enterprise as that. In carrying on the work of the railway or providing freight traffic for the railways from, we will say, Prince Rupert eastward, it would be quite justifiable, according to the same line of argument, that Sir Henry Thornton should organize a fish company up in Prince Rupert; at least he might take one or two million dollars temporarily with the idea of organizing some syndicate with the understanding that if it were successful, he would put the money back again. The argument is no defence for an action of this kind and makes it all the more necessary that some protest should be made by the House to check such a practice as this. The hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) suggested that anyone who would vote in favour of the amendment was simply playing politics. Some of us here fortunately have a short parliamentary record, and we do not need to worry very much about what we did in previous years. I should like to suggest that we have a right, a duty to act on the merits of this question irrespective of who introduced the amendment or any motive that may lie behind it. It was also suggested by the hon. member for Dorchester that anyone who supported the amendment proposed, would be
Supply-Railways-C.N.R.

going back on the principle of public ownership.

My hon. friend might
have understood that, but I do not think I said so.

That is what I
understood. I may have misunderstood. I should, however, like to say that in supporting the amendment proposed, I believe I am doing my best to uphold the principle of public ownership. I believe most firmly in public ownership; but I am not going to be deceived by mere words. I do not want to see set up in this country a public ownership that means very little more than an irresponsible dictatorship. That, it seems to me, is what very readily we may see grow up if we allow this kind of practice to continue.
So far as we have had evidence, produced this evening or at previous sessions of the House, there has been no consent by the minister or by the government, and as the hon. member for St. John City (Mr. Baxter) points out, we have not even had evidence to show that the board itself gave its en-dorsation to the action taken by Sir Henry Thornton. Under these circumstances, I do not see that we have any other course than to vote in favour of the proposed amendment. A previous resolution was turned down on the ground of being out of order; if there were some other way in which we could show our disapproval, possibly we might feel that we like to take that course; but under the circumstances it seems that the only way of doing so is to vote for the amendment, and that I propose to do.

I had not intended to discuss this question, but it seems to me that we might review the situation as has developed. Sir Henry Thornton and the board of directors apparently decided that they wanted a home in Paris. Was that a wise decision? I do not know. I do not think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Woodsworth) who has just taken his seat, knows. I do not think any man in this House knows. I believe the judgment of the board of directors and of Sir Henry Thornton on that question is entitled to greater weight than my judgment. I can conceive that such a thing would be desirable, and I think it would be in the interest of the railroad system. But I do not know much about it. What did he do? He took the advice of an eminent barrister how to go about this matter, the advice of a gentleman whose name has been given us in this House to-day, a gentleman who knew the law, and who knew the facts. He was advised by this gentleman that a certain course 
of procedure was entirely regular and legal, and he adopted that course. Hon. gentlemen have been complaining that they do not know what has taken place; but without knowing the facts, they are giving us their knowledge of what the law is. The gentleman under whose advice this action was taken knew the facts, and when the matter is one of legal opinion, it is very well to apply the law to the facts if you want to get a sound opinion.
That sounds sound.

Then what did he do?
He arranged to guarantee a loan in Paris and hypothecated, as it were, $2,000,000 of the money of the railway company. If the amount had been $2,000, there would not have been any question that he had a right to do this. If he had made an arrangement by which he might rent'an office in Paris or in Luseland, Saskatchewan, the village from which I hail, it would have been within his right and power to do so. The size of the transaction does not make any difference as regards the principle involved if parliament votes money and puts it in the bank. What is the situation? As regards this parliament, or as regards this $2,000,000, no action which we men take can undo what has been done in this case. The performance is over. Shall we interfere when we cannot possibly do any good? Shall we compel the minister to disclose all the transaction and the situation of the parties, and possibly jeopardize the whole performance in order that hon. gentlemen may know some things which they do not know? This thing will keep. We are going to have another session of parliament one of these days. If it is found that an irregular transaction has been made or a losing game has been played, then we can haul Sir Henry Thornton over the coals.
I do not see why we should break right into the midst of this transaction and perhaps jeopardize negotiations, when we have already incurred our part of the responsibility, when our money has been put up and when, if we spill the beans, we shall be the only losers, so far as I qan understand the matter. Why not let events take their course in connection with this transaction in the sincere hope that it will be all right, as I believe it will be? Sir Henry Thornton has been put in charge of this great railway system. He is spending millions upon millions of dollars. We are trusting him to buy locomotives, coal, cars, rails, and to carry on the greatest business transaction on earth to-day. Have we confidence enough in him to believe he can make a deal to rent offices in Paris? If he is not competent to carry this transaction through in what he has

Supply-Railways-C.N.R.
been advised is a perfectly legal and proper manner, then he has no business to be in the place he occupies and we should get rid of him. If he cannot carry through this transaction he cannot run the railroad. I for one have implicit confidence in his ability as a railroad man, and in his integrity as a gentleman, and I believe that the acquisition of this property will in the end prove to be a benefit to the railroad and to the country. .

What is the
system of audit at present applied to the Canadian Government Railways?

It is the same system
that we have always had.

As I recollect,
there used to be a pre-audit in connection with large matters. Is my memory wrong?

I am informed that that
system has not been changed since my hon. friend was Minister of Finance.

I want to find
out if you have to get the auditor's O.K. on your cheque in connection with large expenditures.

I am informed that that
is only in connection with matters where the money is advanced by the government. The same system was in vogue under my hon. friend.
Do I understand that the pre-audit only applies to actual government payments?

By the Auditor General,
yes.
DRAYTON:	What protection is there, who can get a cheque?

The railway has its own
auditors, also an outside firm of very competent auditors.

But I think my hon. friend knows perfectly well that the usual railway operation is that while payments in the discharge of ordinary business can be made-and I am forgetting all abou,t the legal question-when you have an extraordinary paj'ment it can only be made by the board of directors. That being so, how was this money got out without vote or justification?

I am told by the deputy minister that we have the exact system used by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and as required by the Interstate Commerce Commission. All 'the railways are operated under that system.

Does one man
get out a cheque under this system?

It is approved by the proper officer in the department, then it is checked by the comptroller and the treasurer There is no change in the system.
Amendment (Mr. Stevens) negatived: Yeas, 19; Nays, 78.

The
amendment is lost. Shall the resolution carry?
Then, Mr. Chairman, in connection with the resolution, I want the minister to give me the details under (a), the operating deficits for each of the four companies for last year, and the amount spent.
I presume my hon. friend wants the figures for last year?
I am asking for the vote this year and then last year.
I gave him this year's.
May I have it again, please.

Yes.
Operating deficits on Canadian Government Railways, as estimated, $3,000,000.
Canadian Northern Railway, $2,500,000.
Grand Trunk Railway, (nothing).
Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, $4,500,000.
Now, the vote of last year.

This is all in Hansard of some weeks ago.
Canadian Government Railways, $2,496,721.91.
Canadian Northern Railway, $2,946,729.72.
Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, $4,292,866.41.
That is the actual deficit. Will my friend give me the vote last year?
I have not got that.
I asked specially for that information and it was sent over by the deputy, but I was told I had to return it again for use here.

The estimate for last year was:
Canadian Government Railways, $7,000,000.
Canadian Northern Railway, $5,000,000.
Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, $8,000,000.
Then the next, acquisition of property.

I do not seem to have it in that form.

Supply-Railways-C.N.R.
I am trying to keep it just as simple as possible. I am referring to his own vote.
The amount for acquisition of property this year is $2,902,641.
That would be for all the systems?
Yes. We do not seem to have it in the same form for last year.
I think so. The deputy will know whether the form has been changed.
I am informed that the form is not quite what it was last year.

If my memory is not wrong, my hon. friend is incorrect in that. The statute reads exactly the same, and the vote was practically the same. These figures are no good at all unless we can have them as they ought to be-comparative figures.

I am told that the amount was $2,800,000 for last year. Owing to the amalgamation we have one item this year where we had four before, and by adding the four together we get the amount I have mentioned.
May I have the figures of the four votes for last year, please?
I am told that it was under vote 115 of last year.

I think we had better clear that up, because I do not want either to get wrong myself or to start the minister wrong. Now, I have before me item 115 of last year, and as I read it, it is not the item I was referring to. If the minister looks at item 136 of last year he will find that parliament was asked to vote-whether there is anything in it or not I do not know, but I propose to find out-for "acquisition of property, materials and supplies" exactly as we have it this year in the main vote, The item that is now pointed out to me, 115, has to do with miscellaneous railway equipment. Of course, it may be an overlapping. I notice the wording is as follows:
The assistance herein provided may be by way of advances to the Canadian National Rolling Stock Limited or to any company comprised in the Canadian Northern Railway system, or the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway system, or by way of equipment or materials acquired by the minister.
What I want is the amount of the appropriation last year under item (b) of vote 136 of last year. It is exactly the same wording as in the item of this year.
Does my hon. friend want the details of last year?

I am not asking for the details. I am merely asking for the amounts that parliament was asked to give last year according to the various details of last year's vote. There ought to be no mystery about this.

What my hon. friend
wants, then, is a comparison between the amounts appropriated in 1922 and in 1923 for the different purposes set out in the item. I have not the details here, but I will get them for my hon. friend. The difficulty is that last year the amounts were in different votes, while this year they are in one.

To a certain extent that is quite true, but there cannot be a great deal of difficulty, because the wording in each case is the same and all that has to be done is to keep to the same designations of these different details right through.
We will work it out for my hon. friend and let him have it.
I also want to know what was spent on each one of these items under last year's vote. That muse be there too.
There is a little difficulty owing to the two systems but we can work it out. I will see that my hon. friend gets it.
When shall I get it?
We will have it for the first of the week.

What does my hon. friend want to do? We have not the information now. What does he suggest? Is there any other item he wants to pass so that the matter could be discussed on that item. This is the last item I believe, and I am afraid the item cannot carry till I get the figures. I shall very likely want to discuss the figures, and this is the only item on which I could discuss the matter.
We have several items for Railways and Canals on any one of which my hon. friend could have this discussion.
Which one? I thought we had put them all through.

There are several items I know of for Railways and Canals and my hon. friend will be at perfect liberty to discuss

Supply-Rnilwa ys- C.N.R.
this on any one of those. We have spent two days on this item and I should like to get it through.

speechtext:
Items 139 and 140 have not
passed.

Item 140 relates
to the merchant marine. That is a different thing.
We will not maintain that. We have several votes that have not passed yet.
I think they are all passed. We put through several last night for my hon. friend.
There are two votes for Canals that are not passed yet, the vote for maintenance and the Welland ship canal vote. I will keep that for my hon. friend.
How can this matter be discussed on an item for canals?
By consent it could be discussed, of course.

As to that I would say that at an earlier date this session we had a minister who was absolutely anxious, at least so he said, that a certain matter should be discussed, but when the time came he was ruled out of order.
I think it would not be done again in this case, if we have a distinct understanding.
Then we have a distinct understanding that letting this item pass will not preclude the fullest discussion upon the item that my hon. friend picks out, No. 118.
Which item is that?

Item 118. My hon. friend tells me that is open. Then notwithstanding the rules of the House the fullest discussion can take place in connection with these items which my hon. friend now wants to put through, and which I for the purpose of expediting business will not object to passing so long as we have that distinct understanding.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The government would ask the House to give its consent to have that done.
I do not know that that is enough.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We cannot do more.

We have had the government asking for consent before, and I remember the position in whieh the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark) found himself. A similar pledge was given in that case but it could not be carried out. Someone objected. It is quite easy for someone to object to this understanding being carried out. It could easily be blocked. It has been done before.

Further than that I might say that there will be Supplementary Estimates on which it would be fully open for my hon. friend to discuss anything in connection with this item. There can be no question about that.
Perhaps the best thing I can do is to rely on my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals. The understanding is that we let this item go through with the full right to reserve discussion.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
